28, where the company is planning to debut its first touch-screen MacBook.

Apple will also introduce a new low-end MacBook Pro with an M6 chip, a refreshed iMac and a revamped iPad mini with a sharper screen, Bloomberg News has reported.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The new touch MacBooks are expected to include a Dynamic Island interface — like on the iPhone — as well as a sharper display that uses OLED technology.

sources.title: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop - CNBC
passages: Apple announced a product launch event on Oct.
28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles."
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall.
He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.

It will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.
Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors.
Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500.
In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones.
But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024.
Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.

sources.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content - TechCrunch
passages: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

sources.title: Spotify’s new podcast memberships let you pay for extra perks
passages: Users can find Memberships on a podcast’s Spotify page, with the ability to subscribe, pay, and access the exclusive benefits “in just a few taps,” according to Spotify.

That makes this more like a Patreon-style membership system in which fans can choose to give additional support to their favorite creators, and is distinct from the podcast subscription feature that Spotify introduced in 2021.
Podcasters can utilize Memberships alongside other Spotify revenue streams, including ads and the Spotify Partner Program.
To qualify for Memberships, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, and have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and three published episodes.
Spotify is enabling podcast creators to earn more money through the platform by providing their fans with a way to pay to access exclusive content.

Spotify is providing podcasters with tools to analyze and build their Memberships audience, including targeted promotions and free trial offers, alongside community engagement features like member badges, welcome clips, and more.

Spotify is also making it easy for podcasters who manage their subscriptions on other services to try Memberships, allowing them to bring their paywalled content to Spotify via its Open Access feature.

First announced in May, the new Memberships subscription feature is starting to roll out in 34 regions today, allowing podcasters to offer perks including additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads behind a paywall.
Podcast creators can set their pricing options and bundle benefits across multiple subscription tiers, and keep 90 percent of membership revenue.

sources.title: Spotify podcast Memberships let you pay shows directly, with perks like exclusive episodes - How-To Geek
passages: As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.
Creators decide what you get, including free trials as well as exclusive episodes, early access, or reduced ads.
You'll even get a badge if you comment on a given episode.
The catch, as you might expect, is Spotify's cut.
The streaming audio service takes 10% of Memberships revenue, so podcasters have to either accept slightly less money or charge more than they do elsewhere.
This is lower than Apple (30% for the first year, 15% after) and YouTube (30%), but it still means some of your spending isn't going to the podcast itself.
It's now easier to support your favorite podcasts beyond listening to ads.
Spotify is launching Memberships, or paid podcast subscriptions, that can provide perks to loyal listeners.
If that concerns you, some podcasts already make subscriptions available beyond Spotify.
Some offer paid access directly through their websites, while others use services like Patreon (which takes a 5% to 12% cut), Ko-Fi (0% to 5%), or Buy Me a Coffee (5%).
The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

The initial batch of Spotify Memberships podcasts include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society , Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows from YMH Studios.
The option is available whether you're a free or Premium user, and you only share contact details with your express permission.
Hosts can access member data that's useful outside of Spotify, so they can tweak their shows based on listening habits.
As such, the in-Spotify approach might be useful simply by keeping shows running or giving them more opportunities to expand.

passages: Users can find Memberships on a podcast’s Spotify page, with the ability to subscribe, pay, and access the exclusive benefits “in just a few taps,” according to Spotify.

That makes this more like a Patreon-style membership system in which fans can choose to give additional support to their favorite creators, and is distinct from the podcast subscription feature that Spotify introduced in 2021.
Podcasters can utilize Memberships alongside other Spotify revenue streams, including ads and the Spotify Partner Program.
To qualify for Memberships, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, and have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and three published episodes.
Spotify is enabling podcast creators to earn more money through the platform by providing their fans with a way to pay to access exclusive content.

Spotify is providing podcasters with tools to analyze and build their Memberships audience, including targeted promotions and free trial offers, alongside community engagement features like member badges, welcome clips, and more.

Spotify is also making it easy for podcasters who manage their subscriptions on other services to try Memberships, allowing them to bring their paywalled content to Spotify via its Open Access feature.

First announced in May, the new Memberships subscription feature is starting to roll out in 34 regions today, allowing podcasters to offer perks including additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads behind a paywall.
Podcast creators can set their pricing options and bundle benefits across multiple subscription tiers, and keep 90 percent of membership revenue.

sources.title: Spotify podcast Memberships let you pay shows directly, with perks like exclusive episodes - How-To Geek
passages: As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.
Creators decide what you get, including free trials as well as exclusive episodes, early access, or reduced ads.
You'll even get a badge if you comment on a given episode.
The catch, as you might expect, is Spotify's cut.
The streaming audio service takes 10% of Memberships revenue, so podcasters have to either accept slightly less money or charge more than they do elsewhere.
This is lower than Apple (30% for the first year, 15% after) and YouTube (30%), but it still means some of your spending isn't going to the podcast itself.
It's now easier to support your favorite podcasts beyond listening to ads.
Spotify is launching Memberships, or paid podcast subscriptions, that can provide perks to loyal listeners.
If that concerns you, some podcasts already make subscriptions available beyond Spotify.
Some offer paid access directly through their websites, while others use services like Patreon (which takes a 5% to 12% cut), Ko-Fi (0% to 5%), or Buy Me a Coffee (5%).
The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

The initial batch of Spotify Memberships podcasts include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society , Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows from YMH Studios.
The option is available whether you're a free or Premium user, and you only share contact details with your express permission.
Hosts can access member data that's useful outside of Spotify, so they can tweak their shows based on listening habits.
As such, the in-Spotify approach might be useful simply by keeping shows running or giving them more opportunities to expand.

passages: Apple announced a product launch event on Oct.
28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles."
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall.
He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.

It will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.
Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors.
Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500.
In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones.
But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024.
Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.

passages: Despite flagging that “minor safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively,” Han said that TikTok failed to warn parents of the potential dangers of their child using the platform.
TikTok was repeatedly warned by its own staffers about risks its platform posed to child safety, according to court records obtained by NPR.

The publication reports that employees were frustrated over TikTok executives failing to appropriately act on concerns they raised, including minors bypassing age-restricted content, and appearing in “transactional sexual content” the company could financially benefit from.

One deposition from Reagen Maher, who held senior safety and investigations positions between 2021 and 2024, described flagging the prevalence of “transactional sexual content” to then-TikTok CEO V Pappas, regarding minors stripping on TikTok’s Live feature in exchange for “gifts” that can be converted into real currency.

sources.title: TikTok staff raised child safety alarms. Court records show executives failed to act - NPR
passages: TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content.
Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.
Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.
Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime.
TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.
NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents.
After extended communications, the company declined to provide a statement for this story.
It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives.
Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material.
Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial.

In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.
Yet, according to Maher's testimony, a loophole existed in which children could access an 18-plus version of TikTok if they signed up via Google, Facebook or Instagram.

In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively."
The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material.
It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

TikTok, alongside Meta, Google and Snap, is a defendant in multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 to coordinate hundreds of lawsuits alleging that the social media platforms are designed to be harmful to users under 18, and that the companies knew their products carried risks that they did not disclose.
In May, TikTok agreed to pay $8 million to settle a youth mental health and addiction lawsuit brought by a school district in rural Kentucky.

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.
In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.
In most countries, 13 is the minimum age for an account.
The company says it also analyzes data associated with an account to identify those where the stated age may be incorrect.
In these cases, accounts can be sent for human review and potentially placed in a different age-appropriate experience.

extraction.body: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said . The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team. DHS orders removal of DeepSeek AI from federal civilian agencies and bans new contracts. Order cites security concerns and threat vectors; applies to affiliates and third-party services using DeepSeek. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, and it also blocked civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The order, dating back to late July, applied to federal civilian agencies including the departments of the Treasury, State and Justice, while excluding the Department of Defense. The DHS notice in the Federal Register alleged that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including concerns that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data. Mao Ning, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson, said China would “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked about the U.S. ban at a regular press conference. The U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China, with AI expected to be on the agenda. The DHS order warned that using DeepSeek’s AI models could result in sensitive government information being transferred to China, potentially exposing intelligence concerning American citizens and government programmes. The DHS also raised concerns that the models could contain malware or other security weaknesses, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek’s iOS application. The notice described a compliance requirement that executive agencies can request exemptions, including extensions to the compliance deadline, by submitting written justifications to the DHS within 60 days of the order’s issuance. The Department of Homeland Security said the use of DeepSeek AI tools “could lead to the transfer of sensitive data to (China) if used by U.S. government employees or contractors,” and it warned that DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. The U.S. government said the directive applies to all products from the Chinese AI leader, as well as third-party services using its models, while the order does not establish a global ban on Chinese models or prevent independent researchers from studying their capabilities. China’s foreign ministry told Reuters that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies, with Mao Ning saying China “consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues.” The U.S. ban framed DeepSeek as a national security risk by alleging that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including that DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC and that the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure. The DHS order required agencies to remove versions put into place prior to the ban and to check that they had not already been compromised, while also warning organizations to monitor the flow of traffic in and out of the agency and implement enhanced logging and controls for relevant systems. The order also barred DeepSeek from future procurements and extended the restriction beyond DeepSeek itself to third-party products and services developed using its implementations, raising questions about software provenance and supply-chain compliance. The DHS order did not immediately prompt a response from DeepSeek, and the order’s scope remained limited to federal civilian agencies’ information technology systems and procurement activities rather than a general prohibition on private companies or individual users. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said . The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove products developed by Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) startup DeepSeek from their information technology systems and barred them from procuring such products, according to a federal notice released Monday.

The department said the order was issued under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 following a review of a recommendation by the Federal Acquisition Security Council and related evidence.

The South Korean government also moved to restrict the use of DeepSeek in February 2025, with its foreign, trade and defense ministries blocking access to the Chinese AI service on government computers amid concerns over user data collection and potential information leaks.
The restrictions also cover third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.

The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
“We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.

Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week .
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China.

Order cites security concerns and threat vectors; applies to affiliates and third-party services using DeepSeek. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, and it also blocked civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The order, dating back to late July, applied to federal civilian agencies including the departments of the Treasury, State and Justice, while excluding the Department of Defense. The DHS notice in the Federal Register alleged that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including concerns that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data. Mao Ning, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson, said China would “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked about the U.S. ban at a regular press conference. The U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China, with AI expected to be on the agenda. The DHS order warned that using DeepSeek’s AI models could result in sensitive government information being transferred to China, potentially exposing intelligence concerning American citizens and government programmes. The DHS also raised concerns that the models could contain malware or other security weaknesses, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek’s iOS application. The notice described a compliance requirement that executive agencies can request exemptions, including extensions to the compliance deadline, by submitting written justifications to the DHS within 60 days of the order’s issuance. The Department of Homeland Security said the use of DeepSeek AI tools “could lead to the transfer of sensitive data to (China) if used by U.S. government employees or contractors,” and it warned that DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. The U.S. government said the directive applies to all products from the Chinese AI leader, as well as third-party services using its models, while the order does not establish a global ban on Chinese models or prevent independent researchers from studying their capabilities. China’s foreign ministry told Reuters that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies, with Mao Ning saying China “consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues.” The U.S. ban framed DeepSeek as a national security risk by alleging that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including that DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC and that the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure. The DHS order required agencies to remove versions put into place prior to the ban and to check that they had not already been compromised, while also warning organizations to monitor the flow of traffic in and out of the agency and implement enhanced logging and controls for relevant systems. The order also barred DeepSeek from future procurements and extended the restriction beyond DeepSeek itself to third-party products and services developed using its implementations, raising questions about software provenance and supply-chain compliance. The DHS order did not immediately prompt a response from DeepSeek, and the order’s scope remained limited to federal civilian agencies’ information technology systems and procurement activities rather than a general prohibition on private companies or individual users. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said .

Apple's joined the smart home category with the new HomeView, but Amazon isn't moving out anytime soon.
Article updated on October 16, 2026, 11:25 am EDT

No smart home is complete without a hub to manage it, and for a long time, Amazon’s Echo line or Google’s home system was the go-to choice. Apple has finally entered the smart home market with the launch of the HomeView , a direct competitor to the aforementioned brands, and we’ve recently gone hands-on with it.
Also: Apple’s $299 HomeView smart hub is here: 8 highlights, including the wall model

The new device resembles an iPad and is a control center for all your connected smart home devices, including any smart speakers, video doorbells, or smart locks — all of which Apple also announced. So who’s it really for, and how does it compare to popular options like Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) from 2025? Here’s what you should know before making that preorder.

If you’re a die-hard Apple user who’s been waiting for Apple’s new home products, this launch is for you. The HomeView expands Apple’s traditional ecosystem, taking it one step further by bringing many of your favorite Apple features to a smart home hub. It syncs Siri, creates unique profiles for members of your family, tracks locations with FindMy, delivers Intercom messages, and more.
Also: I saw Apple’s HomeView, HomePod Mini 2, and Apple TV 4K – and I’m sold on one

However, chances are, if you’re eyeing the HomeView for your smart home hub, you’re aware there may be extra costs associated with it. For starters, if you want to mount the HomeView, it’ll run you up to $130, depending on the mount you choose. Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t. If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home.

If Siri is your go-to pocket companion, there’s no doubt that you’ll want to add Siri to your home’s hub. Plus, if you want seamless compatibility between devices like your iPhone and your smart home hub, this is the best way to do it. You’ll be able to take FaceTime calls, check locations, and more, as you would on your iPhone, right from Apple’s HomeView.

If you want a smart hub, but don’t want to spend $299 (or more), Amazon’s Echo Show 8 is an all-around better choice. It’s already cheaper, plus it’s not uncommon to see the device discounted even further depending on the time of year. It was just on sale during Prime Day, and it has sold for as low as $125. That’s a great deal on a smart home hub that seamlessly integrates with Alexa and Echo devices, as well as security systems like Ring. If you’re evaluating primarily on price, the Echo Show 8 wins hands-down.

Smart hubs are often the starting point to expand one’s home’s technological offerings. If you foresee yourself purchasing more types of compatible smart accessories along the way, I also have to pay a nod to Alexa’s Echo Show 8 (and family). Amazon’s Echo lineup includes speakers, alarm clocks, displays, lights, and truly takes a well-rounded, robust approach to elevating your home.

Plus, Echo devices and the Alexa system are compatible with other smart devices, like various plugs, sensors, and monitors. Eventually, Apple’s products will likely share wider compatibility, but as it stands right now, the Echo device offerings offer numerous arrangements for many different needs, and the compatibility with Alexa makes it that much better.
Also: Renting? These 2 new Apple smart home devices are worth your money (and these 5 are not)

And if you already have several Alexa-compatible devices? It makes sense to continue with items like the Echo Show 8. And if the Echo Show 8 isn’t your jam — that’s OK. Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes.

Apple’s HomeKit will likely catch up in its compatibility offerings with other smart home products on the market, but if you need max compatibility and variety right now, Amazon and its suite of Echo Show offerings are where it’s at.

I’m a big fan of using tech until it’s no longer functioning (or it no longer meets my needs). I have two Alexa speakers and an Echo Show 5 in my home, and my security sensors and cameras are set up through Ring, which is already compatible with my Amazon devices.

But I’m no stranger to Apple’s ecosystem, either. I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper. But since I already have a smart home hub and security setup I’m happy with, I see no reason to spend more money on an all new setup.
Also: How Apple’s video doorbell privacy compares to Ring, Wyze, and Blink

If you’re a first-time smart home hub buyer, or you’re really set on having a seamless Apple ecosystem, it makes sense. But my general consensus is that Amazon and Google have spent years in the smart home market building and refining great products at better price points than Apple — especially if you find them on sale. You can also bet Apple’s Home lineup won’t be discounted very often, much like the rest of Apple’s products.

sources.title: I saw Apple's HomeView early — 7 things you need to know about the new smart home display - Tom's Guide
passages: I got an early look at Apple's new $299 smart home display ahead of its official announcement, and what struck is that HomeView doesn't feel like an iPad attached to a speaker or an oversized Apple Watch.

Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.”
Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home.
You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously.
The more I saw of HomeView, the more I realized Apple is serious about giving its smart home ecosystem something it's been missing all along: a centerpiece.
When it comes to controlling smart home devices, an optimally-placed, wall-mounted control center tends to be a preferred interface.
Apple has spent years making products for just about every part of our lives.
There's an iPhone in our pockets, an Apple Watch on our wrists, AirPods in our ears, Macs on our desks and an Apple TV in our living rooms.
But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment.
The tabletop HomeView comes with a speaker base featuring a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, along with two full-range drivers in the tilting display itself.
Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups.

Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life.
No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones.
Between FaceTime, recipes, music, photos and personalized information, there's plenty here for someone who hasn't invested much in smart home technology.
And for those who have, HomeView could be the missing link that brings everything together.
Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces.
Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly.
That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device.
HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits.
That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered.
That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house.

Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions.
Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events.
Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message.
Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone.
HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls.
But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Apple has spent years making products for just about every part of our lives. There's an iPhone in our pockets, an Apple Watch on our wrists, AirPods in our ears, Macs on our desks and an Apple TV in our living rooms. But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment. Apple HomeView might finally be it. I got an early look at Apple's new $299 smart home display ahead of its official announcement, and what struck is that HomeView doesn't feel like an iPad attached to a speaker or an oversized Apple Watch. Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.” Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life. Between its personalized interface, surprisingly clever cooking features and new Siri AI capabilities, I came away from the demonstration with a breakdown of these seven features that stand out most. Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly. That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device. Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events. We've heard plenty about how Apple is making Siri smarter with personal context, but Apple's demonstration gave me a more tangible example of what that means. Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message. Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone. The same intelligence can help with calendar requests, questions about everyday topics and other tasks that would typically send you reaching for your phone. Apple says Siri requests are processed on HomeView’s A18 processor, while relevant personal context is retrieved from your iPhone (15 Pro or newer supporting Apple Intelligence.) It's an interesting approach because your iPhone essentially remains the keeper of your personal information, even when you're interacting with another device, but only you can request the use of personal context. When I’ve used Amazon’s smart displays in the past, it's been, primarily, to follow recipes. Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions. You can AirDrop a recipe from your iPhone or search for one directly using Safari, or using personal context, ask for a recipe sent to you in iMessage or Mail to be surfaced. Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces. There are clock faces, modular layouts with widgets, a moving Flow face that reminded me of a lava lamp and even an animated Snoopy face. The Photos face is especially appealing. You can display images of specific people, places or albums, including shared albums, and have them rotate throughout the day. As is the case for iPhone wallpapers, Portrait photos look particularly dynamic. HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits. That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered. That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house. HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls. I can see this being particularly convenient in a kitchen, where you might want to chat with someone while preparing dinner, or in a living room where several family members want to join the same call. You can also hand off FaceTime calls from your other Apple devices. No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones. Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home. You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously. But Apple isn't just introducing a new way to control existing Matter-equipped accessories. It's also teaming up with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric on an entirely new lineup of products called the Apple Home Collection. Apple has spent years making products for just about every part of our lives. There's an iPhone in our pockets, an Apple Watch on our wrists, AirPods in our ears, Macs on our desks and an Apple TV in our living rooms. But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment. Apple HomeView might finally be it.

I got an early look at Apple's new $299 smart home display ahead of its official announcement, and what struck is that HomeView doesn't feel like an iPad attached to a speaker or an oversized Apple Watch. Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.”

Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life.
Between its personalized interface, surprisingly clever cooking features and new Siri AI capabilities, I came away from the demonstration with a breakdown of these seven features that stand out most.

Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly. That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device.
Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events.
We've heard plenty about how Apple is making Siri smarter with personal context, but Apple's demonstration gave me a more tangible example of what that means.
Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message. Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone.
The same intelligence can help with calendar requests, questions about everyday topics and other tasks that would typically send you reaching for your phone.
Apple says Siri requests are processed on HomeView’s A18 processor, while relevant personal context is retrieved from your iPhone (15 Pro or newer supporting Apple Intelligence.)

It's an interesting approach because your iPhone essentially remains the keeper of your personal information, even when you're interacting with another device, but only you can request the use of personal context.

When I’ve used Amazon’s smart displays in the past, it's been, primarily, to follow recipes. Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions.
You can AirDrop a recipe from your iPhone or search for one directly using Safari, or using personal context, ask for a recipe sent to you in iMessage or Mail to be surfaced.
Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces.
There are clock faces, modular layouts with widgets, a moving Flow face that reminded me of a lava lamp and even an animated Snoopy face.

The Photos face is especially appealing. You can display images of specific people, places or albums, including shared albums, and have them rotate throughout the day. As is the case for iPhone wallpapers, Portrait photos look particularly dynamic.

HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits. That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered. That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house.
HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls.

I can see this being particularly convenient in a kitchen, where you might want to chat with someone while preparing dinner, or in a living room where several family members want to join the same call.
You can also hand off FaceTime calls from your other Apple devices.
No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones.

Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home. You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously.

There is a specific issue with the Facebook in-app browser intermittently making requests to websites without cookies that had previously been set. This appears to be a defect in the browser which should be addressed soon. The simplest approach to avoid this problem is to continue to use the Facebook app but not use the in-app browser. This can be done through the following steps: 1. Open the settings menu by clicking the hamburger menu in the top right 2. Choose “App Settings” from the menu 3. Turn on the option “Links Open Externally” (This will use the device’s default browser) Enabling Cookies in Internet Explorer 7, 8 & 9 1. Open the Internet Browser 2. Click Tools > Internet Options > Privacy > Advanced 3. Check Override automatic cookie handling 4. For First-party Cookies and Third-party Cookies click Accept 5. Click OK and OK Enabling Cookies in Firefox 1. Open the Firefox browser 2. Click Tools > Options > Privacy > Use custom settings for history 3. Check Accept cookies from sites 4. Check Accept third party cookies 5. Select Keep until: they expire 6. Click OK Enabling Cookies in Google Chrome 1. Open the Google Chrome browser 2. Click Tools > Options > Privacy Options > Under the Hood > Content Settings 3. Check Allow local data to be set 4. Uncheck Block third-party cookies from being set 5. Uncheck Clear cookies 6. Close all Enabling Cookies in Mobile Safari (iPhone, iPad) 1. Go to the Home screen by pressing the Home button or by unlocking your phone/iPad 2. Select the Settings icon. 3. Select Safari from the settings menu. 4. Select ‘accept cookies’ from the safari menu. 5. Select ‘from visited’ from the accept cookies menu. 6. Press the home button to return the the iPhone home screen. 7. Select the Safari icon to return to Safari. 8. Before the cookie settings change will take effect, Safari must restart. To restart Safari press and hold the Home button (for around five seconds) until the iPhone/iPad display goes blank and the home screen appears. 9. Select the Safari icon to return to Safari.

coreStoryFacts.text: The new device resembles an iPad and is a control center for all your connected smart home devices, including any smart speakers, video doorbells, or smart locks — all of which Apple also announced.
So who’s it really for, and how does it compare to popular options like Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) from 2025?
Here’s what you should know before making that preorder.
It’s already cheaper, plus it’s not uncommon to see the device discounted even further depending on the time of year.
It was just on sale during Prime Day, and it has sold for as low as $125.
That’s a great deal on a smart home hub that seamlessly integrates with Alexa and Echo devices, as well as security systems like Ring.
Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t.

If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home.
Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes.
I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper.
Apple has finally entered the smart home market with the launch of the HomeView , a direct competitor to the aforementioned brands, and we’ve recently gone hands-on with it.

Apple's joined the smart home category with the new HomeView, but Amazon isn't moving out anytime soon.
Article updated on October 16, 2026, 11:25 am EDT

No smart home is complete without a hub to manage it, and for a long time, Amazon’s Echo line or Google’s home system was the go-to choice. Apple has finally entered the smart home market with the launch of the HomeView , a direct competitor to the aforementioned brands, and we’ve recently gone hands-on with it.
Also: Apple’s $299 HomeView smart hub is here: 8 highlights, including the wall model

The new device resembles an iPad and is a control center for all your connected smart home devices, including any smart speakers, video doorbells, or smart locks — all of which Apple also announced. So who’s it really for, and how does it compare to popular options like Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) from 2025? Here’s what you should know before making that preorder.

If you’re a die-hard Apple user who’s been waiting for Apple’s new home products, this launch is for you. The HomeView expands Apple’s traditional ecosystem, taking it one step further by bringing many of your favorite Apple features to a smart home hub. It syncs Siri, creates unique profiles for members of your family, tracks locations with FindMy, delivers Intercom messages, and more.
Also: I saw Apple’s HomeView, HomePod Mini 2, and Apple TV 4K – and I’m sold on one

However, chances are, if you’re eyeing the HomeView for your smart home hub, you’re aware there may be extra costs associated with it. For starters, if you want to mount the HomeView, it’ll run you up to $130, depending on the mount you choose. Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t. If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home.

If Siri is your go-to pocket companion, there’s no doubt that you’ll want to add Siri to your home’s hub. Plus, if you want seamless compatibility between devices like your iPhone and your smart home hub, this is the best way to do it. You’ll be able to take FaceTime calls, check locations, and more, as you would on your iPhone, right from Apple’s HomeView.

If you want a smart hub, but don’t want to spend $299 (or more), Amazon’s Echo Show 8 is an all-around better choice. It’s already cheaper, plus it’s not uncommon to see the device discounted even further depending on the time of year. It was just on sale during Prime Day, and it has sold for as low as $125. That’s a great deal on a smart home hub that seamlessly integrates with Alexa and Echo devices, as well as security systems like Ring. If you’re evaluating primarily on price, the Echo Show 8 wins hands-down.

Smart hubs are often the starting point to expand one’s home’s technological offerings. If you foresee yourself purchasing more types of compatible smart accessories along the way, I also have to pay a nod to Alexa’s Echo Show 8 (and family). Amazon’s Echo lineup includes speakers, alarm clocks, displays, lights, and truly takes a well-rounded, robust approach to elevating your home.

Plus, Echo devices and the Alexa system are compatible with other smart devices, like various plugs, sensors, and monitors. Eventually, Apple’s products will likely share wider compatibility, but as it stands right now, the Echo device offerings offer numerous arrangements for many different needs, and the compatibility with Alexa makes it that much better.
Also: Renting? These 2 new Apple smart home devices are worth your money (and these 5 are not)

And if you already have several Alexa-compatible devices? It makes sense to continue with items like the Echo Show 8. And if the Echo Show 8 isn’t your jam — that’s OK. Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes.

Apple’s HomeKit will likely catch up in its compatibility offerings with other smart home products on the market, but if you need max compatibility and variety right now, Amazon and its suite of Echo Show offerings are where it’s at.

I’m a big fan of using tech until it’s no longer functioning (or it no longer meets my needs). I have two Alexa speakers and an Echo Show 5 in my home, and my security sensors and cameras are set up through Ring, which is already compatible with my Amazon devices.

But I’m no stranger to Apple’s ecosystem, either. I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper. But since I already have a smart home hub and security setup I’m happy with, I see no reason to spend more money on an all new setup.
Also: How Apple’s video doorbell privacy compares to Ring, Wyze, and Blink

If you’re a first-time smart home hub buyer, or you’re really set on having a seamless Apple ecosystem, it makes sense. But my general consensus is that Amazon and Google have spent years in the smart home market building and refining great products at better price points than Apple — especially if you find them on sale. You can also bet Apple’s Home lineup won’t be discounted very often, much like the rest of Apple’s products.

Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.”
Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home.
You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously.
The more I saw of HomeView, the more I realized Apple is serious about giving its smart home ecosystem something it's been missing all along: a centerpiece.
When it comes to controlling smart home devices, an optimally-placed, wall-mounted control center tends to be a preferred interface.
Apple has spent years making products for just about every part of our lives.
There's an iPhone in our pockets, an Apple Watch on our wrists, AirPods in our ears, Macs on our desks and an Apple TV in our living rooms.
But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment.
The tabletop HomeView comes with a speaker base featuring a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, along with two full-range drivers in the tilting display itself.
Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups.

Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life.
No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones.
Between FaceTime, recipes, music, photos and personalized information, there's plenty here for someone who hasn't invested much in smart home technology.
And for those who have, HomeView could be the missing link that brings everything together.
Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces.
Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly.
That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device.
HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits.
That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered.
That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house.

Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions.
Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events.
Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message.
Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone.
HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls.
But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be.

But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment. Apple HomeView might finally be it. I got an early look at Apple's new $299 smart home display ahead of its official announcement, and what struck is that HomeView doesn't feel like an iPad attached to a speaker or an oversized Apple Watch. Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.” Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life. Between its personalized interface, surprisingly clever cooking features and new Siri AI capabilities, I came away from the demonstration with a breakdown of these seven features that stand out most. Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly. That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device. Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events. We've heard plenty about how Apple is making Siri smarter with personal context, but Apple's demonstration gave me a more tangible example of what that means. Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message. Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone. The same intelligence can help with calendar requests, questions about everyday topics and other tasks that would typically send you reaching for your phone. Apple says Siri requests are processed on HomeView’s A18 processor, while relevant personal context is retrieved from your iPhone (15 Pro or newer supporting Apple Intelligence.) It's an interesting approach because your iPhone essentially remains the keeper of your personal information, even when you're interacting with another device, but only you can request the use of personal context. When I’ve used Amazon’s smart displays in the past, it's been, primarily, to follow recipes. Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions. You can AirDrop a recipe from your iPhone or search for one directly using Safari, or using personal context, ask for a recipe sent to you in iMessage or Mail to be surfaced. Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces. There are clock faces, modular layouts with widgets, a moving Flow face that reminded me of a lava lamp and even an animated Snoopy face. The Photos face is especially appealing. You can display images of specific people, places or albums, including shared albums, and have them rotate throughout the day. As is the case for iPhone wallpapers, Portrait photos look particularly dynamic. HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits. That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered. That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house. HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls. I can see this being particularly convenient in a kitchen, where you might want to chat with someone while preparing dinner, or in a living room where several family members want to join the same call. You can also hand off FaceTime calls from your other Apple devices. No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones. Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home. You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously. But Apple isn't just introducing a new way to control existing Matter-equipped accessories. It's also teaming up with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric on an entirely new lineup of products called the Apple Home Collection. When it comes to controlling smart home devices, an optimally-placed, wall-mounted control center tends to be a preferred interface. That’s why Apple is introducing two versions of HomeView hardware at the same price. The tabletop HomeView comes with a speaker base featuring a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, along with two full-range drivers in the tilting display itself. Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups. The wall-mounted model, meanwhile, has audio tuned for its placement and is particularly well-suited for smart home controls. It will offer three mounting options, including two in-wall solutions developed with Schneider Electric. The more I saw of HomeView, the more I realized Apple is serious about giving its smart home ecosystem something it's been missing all along: a centerpiece. What's particularly interesting is that HomeView doesn't seem to depend on having a house full of connected gadgets to be useful. Between FaceTime, recipes, music, photos and personalized information, there's plenty here for someone who hasn't invested much in smart home technology. And for those who have, HomeView could be the missing link that brings everything together. There are still some important questions, particularly around how reliably Siri AI handles personal context and how limiting the lack of a traditional App Store in “HomeView Software” might be. But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be. Apple has spent years finding its way into nearly every corner of our lives. With HomeView, it might have finally figured out how to make the home itself feel like an Apple product. That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house.

I can see this being particularly convenient in a kitchen, where you might want to chat with someone while preparing dinner, or in a living room where several family members want to join the same call.

extraction.body: To enable cookies, follow the instructions for your browser below. There is a specific issue with the Facebook in-app browser intermittently making requests to websites without cookies that had previously been set. This appears to be a defect in the browser which should be addressed soon. The simplest approach to avoid this problem is to continue to use the Facebook app but not use the in-app browser. This can be done through the following steps: 1. Open the settings menu by clicking the hamburger menu in the top right 2. Choose “App Settings” from the menu 3. Turn on the option “Links Open Externally” (This will use the device’s default browser) Enabling Cookies in Internet Explorer 7, 8 & 9 1. Open the Internet Browser 2. Click Tools > Internet Options > Privacy > Advanced 3. Check Override automatic cookie handling 4. For First-party Cookies and Third-party Cookies click Accept 5. Click OK and OK Enabling Cookies in Firefox 1. Open the Firefox browser 2. Click Tools > Options > Privacy > Use custom settings for history 3. Check Accept cookies from sites 4. Check Accept third party cookies 5. Select Keep until: they expire 6. Click OK Enabling Cookies in Google Chrome 1. Open the Google Chrome browser 2. Click Tools > Options > Privacy Options > Under the Hood > Content Settings 3. Check Allow local data to be set 4. Uncheck Block third-party cookies from being set 5. Uncheck Clear cookies 6. Close all Enabling Cookies in Mobile Safari (iPhone, iPad) 1. Go to the Home screen by pressing the Home button or by unlocking your phone/iPad 2. Select the Settings icon. 3. Select Safari from the settings menu. 4. Select ‘accept cookies’ from the safari menu. 5. Select ‘from visited’ from the accept cookies menu. 6. Press the home button to return the the iPhone home screen. 7. Select the Safari icon to return to Safari. 8. Before the cookie settings change will take effect, Safari must restart. To restart Safari press and hold the Home button (for around five seconds) until the iPhone/iPad display goes blank and the home screen appears. 9. Select the Safari icon to return to Safari.

sources.title: JPMorgan brings deposit token to ethereum for institutional clients - The Edge Malaysia
passages: JPM Coin — which represents US dollar deposits at the largest US bank — will be made available to the company’s institutional clients on the ethereum network, JPMorgan said in a statement on Monday.

First launched last year on Coinbase Global Inc-affiliated blockchain base, the deposit token allows clients to send and receive money in seconds and 24/7, rather than over several days and only during working hours.
The bank chose to bring the token to ethereum because of its liquidity and existing use among clients, Landriault said.
JPMorgan is one of the more active banks in blockchain development.
It also runs the Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Account network, which allows corporate clients to move dollars, euros, pounds and several other currencies, on the bank’s private blockchain.
The network processes more than US$7 billion in transactions a day, JPMorgan said, a sliver of the roughly US$12 trillion a day its broader payments division handles daily.
(Oct 19): JPMorgan Chase & Co is launching its deposit token on ethereum, extending the lender’s push into blockchain payments as Wall Street grows more comfortable moving money on public networks.
JPMorgan’s expansion comes as banks and other large financial firms seek ways to move assets faster and beyond the limitations of traditional systems by using crypto’s underlying technology.
A company backed by more than 100 corporations including Visa Inc, Stripe Inc, and Mastercard Inc issued a US dollar-pegged stablecoin last month, another form of digital money.

“It’s not just Wall Street going to public chains, but the institutional web3 players getting more embedded and partnering with traditional financial institutions.” JPM Coin’s move onto ethereum underscores that shift, she added.

Moving onto public infrastructure — albeit with limits on who can hold the tokens — brings Wall Street closer to the crypto ecosystem, enabling them to tap into existing pools of liquidity and developer activity.

sources.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content
passages: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

sources.title: Spotify podcast Memberships let you pay shows directly, with perks like exclusive episodes - How-To Geek
passages: As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.
Creators decide what you get, including free trials as well as exclusive episodes, early access, or reduced ads.
You'll even get a badge if you comment on a given episode.
The catch, as you might expect, is Spotify's cut.
The streaming audio service takes 10% of Memberships revenue, so podcasters have to either accept slightly less money or charge more than they do elsewhere.
This is lower than Apple (30% for the first year, 15% after) and YouTube (30%), but it still means some of your spending isn't going to the podcast itself.
It's now easier to support your favorite podcasts beyond listening to ads.
Spotify is launching Memberships, or paid podcast subscriptions, that can provide perks to loyal listeners.
If that concerns you, some podcasts already make subscriptions available beyond Spotify.
Some offer paid access directly through their websites, while others use services like Patreon (which takes a 5% to 12% cut), Ko-Fi (0% to 5%), or Buy Me a Coffee (5%).
The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

The initial batch of Spotify Memberships podcasts include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society , Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows from YMH Studios.
This also helps podcasts extend their reach — they'll theoretically get more paid subscribers than they would if they stuck to the usual crowdfunding methods.
The option is available whether you're a free or Premium user, and you only share contact details with your express permission.
Hosts can access member data that's useful outside of Spotify, so they can tweak their shows based on listening habits.
As such, the in-Spotify approach might be useful simply by keeping shows running or giving them more opportunities to expand.
