sources.title: Spotify Takes on Patreon With New Paid Podcast Memberships - Innovation Village
passages: Spotify wants to make that experience more accessible by bringing paid memberships directly to its platform, where listeners already discover and stream podcasts.
This approach puts Spotify in closer competition with Patreon and other membership platforms.
However, Spotify’s advantage is that creators can offer paid benefits within an app their audiences may already use every day.
If listeners are willing to pay for more access, community and convenience, Spotify hopes memberships will help turn that loyalty into recurring revenue.
The streaming platform has launched a new Memberships feature that allows eligible podcast creators to charge fans for additional benefits directly through Spotify .
Spotify says eligible creators will keep 90% of membership revenue, giving podcasters another option for building a sustainable business.
Spotify is also providing creators with audience insights and promotional tools to help them understand their supporters and grow their memberships.
A membership becomes harder to justify when subscribers cannot see a clear difference between the free and paid experiences.

coreStoryFacts.text: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.
As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.
Creators decide what you get, including free trials as well as exclusive episodes, early access, or reduced ads.
You'll even get a badge if you comment on a given episode.
The catch, as you might expect, is Spotify's cut.
The streaming audio service takes 10% of Memberships revenue, so podcasters have to either accept slightly less money or charge more than they do elsewhere.
This is lower than Apple (30% for the first year, 15% after) and YouTube (30%), but it still means some of your spending isn't going to the podcast itself.
It's now easier to support your favorite podcasts beyond listening to ads.
Spotify is launching Memberships, or paid podcast subscriptions, that can provide perks to loyal listeners.
If that concerns you, some podcasts already make subscriptions available beyond Spotify.
Some offer paid access directly through their websites, while others use services like Patreon (which takes a 5% to 12% cut), Ko-Fi (0% to 5%), or Buy Me a Coffee (5%).
The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

The initial batch of Spotify Memberships podcasts include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society , Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows from YMH Studios.
This also helps podcasts extend their reach — they'll theoretically get more paid subscribers than they would if they stuck to the usual crowdfunding methods.
The option is available whether you're a free or Premium user, and you only share contact details with your express permission.
Hosts can access member data that's useful outside of Spotify, so they can tweak their shows based on listening habits.

As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.”
The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally , including the U.S.

This approach puts Spotify in closer competition with Patreon and other membership platforms.
However, Spotify’s advantage is that creators can offer paid benefits within an app their audiences may already use every day.
If listeners are willing to pay for more access, community and convenience, Spotify hopes memberships will help turn that loyalty into recurring revenue.

extraction.body: Spotify is giving podcasters another way to turn loyal listeners into paying supporters, and this time, the offer goes beyond exclusive episodes. The streaming platform has launched a new Memberships feature that allows eligible podcast creators to charge fans for additional benefits directly through Spotify . Instead of relying only on advertising, sponsorships or occasional bonus episodes, creators can build recurring income by offering experiences that make their most dedicated listeners feel closer to their favourite shows. The feature is rolling out across 34 markets, allowing creators to set membership prices and decide what paying fans receive. Spotify says eligible creators will keep 90% of membership revenue, giving podcasters another option for building a sustainable business. Paid podcast subscriptions are not new. Platforms such as Patreon already allow creators to charge fans for exclusive content, behind-the-scenes access and other benefits. Spotify wants to make that experience more accessible by bringing paid memberships directly to its platform, where listeners already discover and stream podcasts. Creators can offer bonus episodes, early access to new releases and reduced advertising. They can also introduce community-focused perks, including member badges and welcome clips, to give subscribers a stronger sense of belonging. That means a podcaster does not necessarily have to produce an entirely separate show to convince listeners to pay. Early access, an ad-light listening experience or a closer connection with the host could be enough to attract some fans. The challenge will be deciding which benefits justify a recurring payment without making free listeners feel as though they are missing out on the entire show. The new membership option is part of Spotify’s wider push to help podcast creators earn money through different channels. Advertising remains an important source of income, but earnings can fluctuate depending on audience size, advertiser demand and the type of content a creator produces. Memberships offer another potential revenue stream because subscribers pay regularly for benefits they value. Spotify is also providing creators with audience insights and promotional tools to help them understand their supporters and grow their memberships. Creators can reach members directly and access tools designed to help them promote their paid offerings. The company also plans to support features such as free trials, giving listeners an opportunity to explore a membership before committing to a payment. This approach puts Spotify in closer competition with Patreon and other membership platforms. However, Spotify’s advantage is that creators can offer paid benefits within an app their audiences may already use every day. The company is not asking podcasters to abandon advertising or sponsorships, either. Memberships can work alongside other revenue streams, giving creators more flexibility in how they fund their shows. The feature could be particularly useful for creators with loyal audiences who regularly return for new episodes. A smaller podcast with an engaged community may find that a group of paying supporters provides more dependable income than chasing larger download numbers alone. Still, not every show will benefit equally. Creators must offer something listeners genuinely value, communicate the benefits clearly and maintain a reliable publishing schedule. A membership becomes harder to justify when subscribers cannot see a clear difference between the free and paid experiences. Eligibility also matters. To qualify for the new feature, podcasters must host their shows through Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 hours of consumption, reach at least 100 listeners or viewers, and have published at least three episodes. The feature is not automatically available to every podcaster. For Nigerian creators, availability is another consideration. Spotify’s podcast monetisation programmes have country-specific eligibility rules, so creators should check the latest requirements before assuming they can activate the new membership feature. Spotify’s move reflects a bigger shift in podcasting. Creators are increasingly looking beyond advertising to build direct relationships with the people who support their work. If listeners are willing to pay for more access, community and convenience, Spotify hopes memberships will help turn that loyalty into recurring revenue. Olusayo Kuti is a writer and researcher,driven to produce engaging content and sharing insightful knowledge

sources.title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant
passages: Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking.
The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number.
The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.
Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers .

With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.
Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer.
Other companies like Meta have also been courting small businesses with AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries .
Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings.
Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.
The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services.
Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats.

The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app. Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon. Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view. To cap off all these changes, Yelp has been thinking about enhancing customer support and business processes through AI. In the new update, the company is releasing a new paid product called Smart Lead Reply, which can reply to customers and engage with them to qualify a lead. Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer. sources.title: Yelp’s AI Assistant Can Call a Restaurant and Join the Waitlist for You - CNET
passages: Just months after launching an updated AI assistant, Yelp Assistant , that can book reservations for you, Yelp is expanding its AI integrations with a new AI agent.
Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes.

As personal and shopping assistants become more widely used, new reports show the hardships faced by both businesses and customers: Businesses must contend with an influx of calls and emails from bots, while human customers must compete with AI agents to make reservations.

“This release is another step forward as we transform Yelp with AI, with updates across every category on Yelp, from booking a table at a restaurant to hiring a pro for a home project,” Akhil Kuduvalli Ramesh, Yelp’s chief product officer, said in a statement.
You can also use Yelp Waitlist to get in line before you arrive.
After you join the line, Yelp Assistant will send you status updates, such as when your table becomes available.
Yelp Assistant’s personalization will also apply to conversations by referencing past chats and your Yelp review history.
For instance, if you’ve recently chatted on Yelp for vegan restaurants near you, the Assistant will ask if you’re interested in more vegan options.
Yelp Assistant now works with OpenTable, allowing you access to thousands of restaurants across the US.
© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.
For further personalization, the app can now reference local weather forecasts when you make reservations, so you don’t book an outdoor patio on a night it’s supposed to pour.
And a new feature, My Lists, lets you save, rank and promote your favorite local businesses, and then Yelp will give you more tailored recommendations based on your lists.

Anthropic is targeting a $1.1 trillion IPO in December 2026 and OpenAI follows in 2027. Space Exploration Technologies Corp (NASDAQ: SPCX) listed last week at US$1.75 trillion. It was the largest IPO in stock market history. And it is just the beginning. Anthropic is targeting a December 2026 public debut at a forecast first-day market cap of approximately US$1.1 trillion, according to the most current forecasts. OpenAI, which filed its own confidential S-1 earlier this month, is expected to follow in early 2027 at a comparable valuation. Together, SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI represent a combined public market value approaching US$4 trillion. For Australian investors who cannot buy any of these stocks on the ASX, the question is what it means for the companies they can buy. The most important consequence of trillion-dollar AI IPOs is not the immediate share price movement in SPCX, Anthropic, or OpenAI. It is the reallocation of institutional capital that follows. The Betashares Space Industry ETF is already living proof of the thesis. The fund launched at $14 per unit on 12 May 2026, well before SpaceX listed. It surged approximately 30% in the weeks leading up to the SpaceX IPO as anticipation built. This served to demonstrate how powerfully public AI IPOs move adjacent listed markets. SpaceX itself will take time to enter the index, but the attention the listing generates flows directly into RCKT's holdings. As Anthropic and OpenAI approach their own listings later this year and in 2027, the same dynamic will play out across AI infrastructure stocks globally. For ASX investors, RCKT captures that excitement in a single trade. NextDC is Australia's largest independent data centre operator and has the most direct relationship with the AI IPO wave of any ASX company. OpenAI is NextDC's foundational customer for its US$7 billion AI data centre campus in Western Sydney. Anthropic's Claude platform is already being deployed by Australian government agencies and critical infrastructure operators who cannot use offshore AI infrastructure. Anthropic's annualised revenue reportedly crossed $47 billion in May 2026, and the company is on track to post its first operating profit in Q2 2026. As Anthropic's public listing raises its enterprise profile globally, the demand for sovereign Australian AI infrastructure will only grow. extraction.body: The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has produced two of the fastest-growing start-ups in history. OpenAI burst onto the scene in late 2022 when it launched ChatGPT, introducing consumers around the world to generative AI. Meanwhile, Anthropic has emerged as a formidable competitor with its Claude models. Both companies' growth has been extraordinary. Following a $122 billion funding round in March, OpenAI reached a valuation of $852 billion, while Anthropic was valued at $965 billion after its Series H round in May. Naturally, AI investors are eager to know when they can buy shares. Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain. Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet ( GOOGL -0.67% ) ( GOOG -0.71% ) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why. One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models. This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous. Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027. These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom. Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini? The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model. This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly. OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate . Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion . At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate. These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis . Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses. While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs. Adam Spatacco has positions in Alphabet and Microsoft. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet and Microsoft. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. extraction.body: The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has produced two of the fastest-growing start-ups in history. OpenAI burst onto the scene in late 2022 when it launched ChatGPT, introducing consumers around the world to generative AI. Meanwhile, Anthropic has emerged as a formidable competitor with its Claude models. Both companies' growth has been extraordinary. Following a $122 billion funding round in March, OpenAI reached a valuation of $852 billion, while Anthropic was valued at $965 billion after its Series H round in May. Naturally, AI investors are eager to know when they can buy shares. Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain. Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet ( GOOGL -0.67% ) ( GOOG -0.71% ) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why. One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models. This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous. Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027. These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom. Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini? The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model. This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly. OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate . Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion . At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate. These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis . Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses. While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs. extraction.body: Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised a $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . TerraPower LLC, a startup founded by Gates, broke ground for construction of its first commercial reactor last week in Wyoming, where a coal plant is shutting down, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft Corp. said on CBS’s Face the Nation . TerraPower has explored simpler, cheaper reactors since 2008 and expects to complete the new reactor in 2030. “I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more,” said Gates, the world’s sixth-richest person according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. TerraPower’s plant, which has backing by the US Department of Energy, was initially expected to be operational in 2028. But that would have meant relying on fuel from Russia, which is “unacceptable now,” Gates said on CNN’s Fareed Zakaria GPS . The reactor design uses liquid sodium as a coolant rather than water and includes molten salt that can store heat to boost its output. TerraPower plans to source reactor fuel from the US and its allies, Gates said. “Coal is being outcompeted by natural gas,” Gates told CNN. “And so what we have to do is compete effectively with natural gas.” Carbon-free nuclear power is increasingly seen as a key part of fighting climate change, and more companies are promoting smaller reactors. Last year, 25 nations at the COP28 climate change conference in Dubai declared an ambition to triple nuclear capacity, according to BloombergNEF.

extraction.body: Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised a $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . extraction.body: Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive. Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night. "It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs. This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue". She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on. According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year. Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold. "I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app." The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker. Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute. "The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes. As you may expect at a dating event many of the singles told us they were keen for that in-real-life or IRL experience. There are a lot of #SingleTok and #Singlelife accounts on TikTok and Instagram reviewing dating events. Candice Gallagher runs an account called @Candilicious and recently went to 10 different dating events in 10 weeks. She describes herself as an entrepreneur and thinks in business terms dating events deliver "much greater return on investment". The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation. "At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater." Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app. These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night. Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating. "I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold." Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again. She is not alone in finding dating expensive. More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date. And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130. Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet. New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club. The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends. Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, says Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters. As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together. And Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL, she says. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app. "What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps." In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation.
"At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater."
Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app.
These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night.
Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating.
"I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold."
Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again.
She is not alone in finding dating expensive.
More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date.
And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130.
Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet.

New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club.
The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends.
Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, says Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters.

As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together.

And Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL, she says. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app.
"What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps."
In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

extraction.body: Dating apps aren’t delivering when it comes to finding a life partner. Single people are getting sick of swiping and abandoning dating apps in droves. That’s left the apps themselves desperately attempting to pivot amidst public backlash against their business premise — to the point of turning their backs on what made them successful in the first place. Tinder, which made billions on the idea that people want to meet one another easily online, has taken to hosting in-person events. Bumble, which just made a deal to go private after years of its stock price tanking, has turned its back on its feminist mission, which used to require women to make the first move. They’re trying anything to keep public trust, despite the fact three-quarters of Americans now believe dating apps have made romance feel transactional, per a 2026 Harris poll . “[The apps] took the friction out of finding someone, but they also took the friction out of exiting, which means that you weren’t getting the depth of the experience,” Boston University business professor Marshall Van Alstyne told The Post. “Initially, they were creating a lot of value to get folks on board [lots of people to potentially date], but now they’ve entered the extractive phase [charging subscription fees], and I think we’re now seeing the consequences.” Business is looking pretty grim. Match Group, which owns Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid, and many other platforms, laid off 13% of their workforce last year, and Bumble 30% last June. Bumble once had 12.5 million users who spent an average of 100 minutes a day swiping, but the app’s paying users fell by almost 17% year-over-year, and revenue dropped 15% during the same period. Since going public in 2021, Bumble has lost 90% of its market value. The struggling app made a deal last Tuesday to go private for $1.3 billion — chump change compared with its $14 billion valuation at its initial public offering. To New York City matchmaker Maria Avgitidis, part of the problem was going public in the first place — shifting obligations away from hooking users up to line shareholder pockets: “[The apps] had to find the equilibrium between providing a good product and also providing positive returns to their shareholders. And sometimes those things are not going to align.” When Bumble was founded in 2014, it positioned itself as a feminist alternative to Tinder, led by a female CEO who put women in control by requiring them to send a message to their matches first. As of August, the app had turned its back on that fundamental premise, and now anyone can send the first message — making it virtually indistinguishable from competitors. Even the female founder and CEO herself, Whitney Wolfe Herd, is stepping aside to make room for two incoming male CEOs upon going private. Bumble did not respond to request for comment. Amy Andersen, the self-described matchmaker of Silicon Valley, believes the apps’ contraction is part of a larger disillusionment with the idea that romance could be made simpler by algorithms. She told The Post she’s noticed a “huge exodus from the apps” that’s escalated in the last three years — even among the techies who literally founded them. “I have had clients literally be the ones who have built the app, but they’re not using it when it comes to their own personal lives,” she said. “The machine professionally dominates their lives, yet when it comes to the intricacies of their personal lives, they’re choosing the human.” Another app trying to reinvent itself is Tinder, which has seen monthly active users decline 7% year-over-year as of March and whose parent company Match Group is increasing Tinder’s marketing budget by $50 million this year. After almost fifteen years in the business of matching people seamlessly online through a swipe, they’re moving into the events space and offering users in-person gatherings on a new tab in the app. Tinder told The Post that they’ve facilitated over 1,700 events so far and hope to reach 75 cities by the end of the year. They seem to have reached an unlikely conclusion: that staying alive in the online dating space might require recreating the sort of social scenarios apps were originally aiming to replace. Tinder has also tried to get people together in groups, rather than on one-on-one dates. They launched “double date mode” in 2025, and last month added group hangouts to their offerings. “We’re building ways to lower the pressure on Tinder,” a spokesperson told The Post. “Ultimately, our goal is to make finding a spark feel more fun, authentic and connected to real life.” The move comes as singles are flocking to more old school methods of finding partners. They’re joining running clubs and pickleball leagues in hopes of finding the one, and setting up their friends with potential matches. Meanwhile, in-person singles events hosted on Eventbrite literally doubled between 2022 and 2025. Disillusioned singles are also trying out good old-fashioned matchmaking — tasking a human, rather than an algorithm, with finding them love. Chris Kumar, CEO of the country’s largest online matchmaking service Tawkify, said his platform has grown 30% year-over-year. The upswing, he says, is part of a larger story of “dating app fatigue” and singles desperately looking for a more substantive alternative. “The apps lost the elegance of what it means to be online and have that spark of connection with someone who swipes on you. That just isn’t exciting anymore,” he said. “So [the apps are trying] to find ways to reinvigorate that hope and that excitement from singles.” The whole transformation seems to point to an uncomfortable conclusion: the future of dating apps may be one where the apps themselves take the back seat, and let singles find one another on their own terms. Its the clearest proof yet that Cupid’s mysterious ways can’t be distilled into an algorthim and true love remains as unpredictable and sometimes elusive as ever.

extraction.body: Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive. Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night. "It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs. This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue". She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on. According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year. Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold. "I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app." The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker. Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute. "The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes. As you may expect at a dating event many of the singles told us they were keen for that in-real-life or IRL experience. There are a lot of #SingleTok and #Singlelife accounts on TikTok and Instagram reviewing dating events. Candice Gallagher runs an account called @Candilicious and recently went to 10 different dating events in 10 weeks. She describes herself as an entrepreneur and thinks in business terms dating events deliver "much greater return on investment". The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation. "At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater." Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app. These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night. Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating. "I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold." Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again. She is not alone in finding dating expensive. More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date. And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130. Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet. New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club. The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends. Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, says Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters. As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together. And Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL, she says. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app. "What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps." In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

extraction.body: Dating apps aren’t delivering when it comes to finding a life partner. Single people are getting sick of swiping and abandoning dating apps in droves. That’s left the apps themselves desperately attempting to pivot amidst public backlash against their business premise — to the point of turning their backs on what made them successful in the first place. Tinder, which made billions on the idea that people want to meet one another easily online, has taken to hosting in-person events. Bumble, which just made a deal to go private after years of its stock price tanking, has turned its back on its feminist mission, which used to require women to make the first move. They’re trying anything to keep public trust, despite the fact three-quarters of Americans now believe dating apps have made romance feel transactional, per a 2026 Harris poll . “[The apps] took the friction out of finding someone, but they also took the friction out of exiting, which means that you weren’t getting the depth of the experience,” Boston University business professor Marshall Van Alstyne told The Post. “Initially, they were creating a lot of value to get folks on board [lots of people to potentially date], but now they’ve entered the extractive phase [charging subscription fees], and I think we’re now seeing the consequences.” Business is looking pretty grim. Match Group, which owns Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid, and many other platforms, laid off 13% of their workforce last year, and Bumble 30% last June. Bumble once had 12.5 million users who spent an average of 100 minutes a day swiping, but the app’s paying users fell by almost 17% year-over-year, and revenue dropped 15% during the same period. Since going public in 2021, Bumble has lost 90% of its market value. The struggling app made a deal last Tuesday to go private for $1.3 billion — chump change compared with its $14 billion valuation at its initial public offering. To New York City matchmaker Maria Avgitidis, part of the problem was going public in the first place — shifting obligations away from hooking users up to line shareholder pockets: “[The apps] had to find the equilibrium between providing a good product and also providing positive returns to their shareholders. And sometimes those things are not going to align.” When Bumble was founded in 2014, it positioned itself as a feminist alternative to Tinder, led by a female CEO who put women in control by requiring them to send a message to their matches first. As of August, the app had turned its back on that fundamental premise, and now anyone can send the first message — making it virtually indistinguishable from competitors. Even the female founder and CEO herself, Whitney Wolfe Herd, is stepping aside to make room for two incoming male CEOs upon going private. Bumble did not respond to request for comment. Amy Andersen, the self-described matchmaker of Silicon Valley, believes the apps’ contraction is part of a larger disillusionment with the idea that romance could be made simpler by algorithms. She told The Post she’s noticed a “huge exodus from the apps” that’s escalated in the last three years — even among the techies who literally founded them. “I have had clients literally be the ones who have built the app, but they’re not using it when it comes to their own personal lives,” she said. “The machine professionally dominates their lives, yet when it comes to the intricacies of their personal lives, they’re choosing the human.” Another app trying to reinvent itself is Tinder, which has seen monthly active users decline 7% year-over-year as of March and whose parent company Match Group is increasing Tinder’s marketing budget by $50 million this year. After almost fifteen years in the business of matching people seamlessly online through a swipe, they’re moving into the events space and offering users in-person gatherings on a new tab in the app. Tinder told The Post that they’ve facilitated over 1,700 events so far and hope to reach 75 cities by the end of the year. They seem to have reached an unlikely conclusion: that staying alive in the online dating space might require recreating the sort of social scenarios apps were originally aiming to replace. Tinder has also tried to get people together in groups, rather than on one-on-one dates. They launched “double date mode” in 2025, and last month added group hangouts to their offerings. “We’re building ways to lower the pressure on Tinder,” a spokesperson told The Post. “Ultimately, our goal is to make finding a spark feel more fun, authentic and connected to real life.” The move comes as singles are flocking to more old school methods of finding partners. They’re joining running clubs and pickleball leagues in hopes of finding the one, and setting up their friends with potential matches. Meanwhile, in-person singles events hosted on Eventbrite literally doubled between 2022 and 2025. Disillusioned singles are also trying out good old-fashioned matchmaking — tasking a human, rather than an algorithm, with finding them love. Chris Kumar, CEO of the country’s largest online matchmaking service Tawkify, said his platform has grown 30% year-over-year. The upswing, he says, is part of a larger story of “dating app fatigue” and singles desperately looking for a more substantive alternative. “The apps lost the elegance of what it means to be online and have that spark of connection with someone who swipes on you. That just isn’t exciting anymore,” he said. “So [the apps are trying] to find ways to reinvigorate that hope and that excitement from singles.” The whole transformation seems to point to an uncomfortable conclusion: the future of dating apps may be one where the apps themselves take the back seat, and let singles find one another on their own terms. Its the clearest proof yet that Cupid’s mysterious ways can’t be distilled into an algorthim and true love remains as unpredictable and sometimes elusive as ever.

passages: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday.
Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions.
As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others.
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people.
The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.
“What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search.
With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.
People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link.

In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

sources.title: Early users delete personal AI agents over privacy scares and blunders
passages: But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information.
For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving.

Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively.

Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran.
"I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said.
Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share.
It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data.
It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.
Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them.

Many early adopters of Instinct and Meta's Muse have said the digital assistants saved them time and money by searching the web, managing inboxes and calendars, disputing bills, booking travel, and making purchases.
Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users.
"But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared.
Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data.

extraction.body: Many early adopters of Instinct and Meta's Muse have said the digital assistants saved them time and money by searching the web, managing inboxes and calendars, disputing bills, booking travel, and making purchases. For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving. Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively. Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran. Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
