sources.title: TikTok staff raised child safety alarms. Court records show executives failed to act - NPR
passages: TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content.
Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.
Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.
Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime.
TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.
NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents.
After extended communications, the company declined to provide a statement for this story.
It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives.
Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material.
Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial.

In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively."
The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material.
It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

TikTok, alongside Meta, Google and Snap, is a defendant in multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 to coordinate hundreds of lawsuits alleging that the social media platforms are designed to be harmful to users under 18, and that the companies knew their products carried risks that they did not disclose.

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.

Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.)
They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony.
Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in.
In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.
TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing.

In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough." Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the March court filings. The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules. Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K. "If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut." Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law. Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering. If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena. In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions. TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices. The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content. The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit. Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content. The app first became prominent in 2018, when ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, acquired Musical.ly, a platform for creating short music and lip-syncing videos that was popular with teen users in the U.S. Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.) Soon after the 2018 merger with Musical.ly, the company was keen to determine the demographics of its user base in the U.S. But the court documents show that it held off on researching the question in an effort to avoid government scrutiny over having children under the age of 13 on the platform. In testimony concerning a 2018 discussion between Adam Wang, who was the Head of TikTok Live at the time, and Alex Zhu, co-founder of Musical.ly and then president of TikTok following the acquisition of Musical.ly, the two discussed a survey. They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony. Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in. COPPA is a federal law that protects the online privacy and personal information of children under 13. It generally prohibits companies from collecting children's personal information without verifiable parental consent. TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing. Among the most serious concerns raised in the testimony was TikTok's handling of content related to suicide and self-harm for young users. Testimony from Eric Han , who was TikTok's head of safety from April 2019 through June 2023, detailed internal chats he'd engaged in concerning "rabbit holes" — the company's term for when the algorithm gets stuck showing the user the same type of content over and over again. Han said he became aware of this problem in April 2020, and acknowledged that rabbit holes could be harmful, such as ones focusing on body image or suicide, and could violate TikTok's policies. An internal report authored and circulated by Han in 2020 and discussed in his testimony stated that there is a "Real contagion effect. Suicidal ideation and behavior, and the way that it is talked about on the platform." In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively." Despite this, Han said the platform did not warn parents of the potential dangers of TikTok.

In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough." Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published. The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules. Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K. "If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit. Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content. The app first became prominent in 2018, when ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, acquired Musical.ly, a platform for creating short music and lip-syncing videos that was popular with teen users in the U.S. Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.) Soon after the 2018 merger with Musical.ly, the company was keen to determine the demographics of its user base in the U.S. But the court documents show that it held off on researching the question in an effort to avoid government scrutiny over having children under the age of 13 on the platform. In testimony concerning a 2018 discussion between Adam Wang, who was the Head of TikTok Live at the time, and Alex Zhu, co-founder of Musical.ly and then president of TikTok following the acquisition of Musical.ly, the two discussed a survey. They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony. Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in. COPPA is a federal law that protects the online privacy and personal information of children under 13. It generally prohibits companies from collecting children's personal information without verifiable parental consent. TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing. Among the most serious concerns raised in the testimony was TikTok's handling of content related to suicide and self-harm for young users. Testimony from Eric Han , who was TikTok's head of safety from April 2019 through June 2023, detailed internal chats he'd engaged in concerning "rabbit holes" — the company's term for when the algorithm gets stuck showing the user the same type of content over and over again. Han said he became aware of this problem in April 2020, and acknowledged that rabbit holes could be harmful, such as ones focusing on body image or suicide, and could violate TikTok's policies. An internal report authored and circulated by Han in 2020 and discussed in his testimony stated that there is a "Real contagion effect. Suicidal ideation and behavior, and the way that it is talked about on the platform." In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively." Despite this, Han said the platform did not warn parents of the potential dangers of TikTok.

sources.title: Aikido Security launches Noon to protect employees from AI-powered social engineering - The Manila Times
passages: "We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security.
"But companies don't just need to protect the software they build.
AI is making social engineering more convincing and easier to scale, while fundamentally changing how employees work.
With Noon, we're bringing the same approach to workforce security: one platform, less complexity, and protection for every employee, not just those building software."
20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aikido Security today announced the launch of Noon , a dedicated workforce security business that extends its protection beyond software to the people using it.
Noon addresses these threats by bringing email protection, device protection, AI governance and phishing simulation training together in one platform.

Noon's platform is being built on two acquisitions Aikido completed in September 2026: Poland-based Cyberly, founded in 2024, which brought AI-driven attack simulations and AI usage visibility, and Belgium-based Outkept, founded in 2020, which brought email security and phishing awareness training.
Before the acquisitions, Cyberly protected more than 300,000 employees across 200-plus organizations, while Outkept served more than 1,000 organizations and 250,000 users across 100-plus countries.
Aikido's unified security platform secures application testing, code, cloud and runtime, helping teams to reduce risk without slowing down development.

Aikido is the fastest-ever European cybersecurity company to reach unicorn status and is trusted by over 150,000 teams, with a global customer base including SoundCloud, Niantic, Runway, Handshake and Deel.
Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that mobile social engineering attacks, including fraudulent texts and voice calls, succeeded 40% more often than email phishing.
Noon brings employee security into one platform, replacing the separate tools many organizations piece together today:
Yet the security industry has long treated software and workforce security as two separate worlds," said Alex Horlach, co-founder of Cyberly.
The founding teams of both companies continue at Noon.
Cyberly's four co-founders, Alex Horlach, Evgeny Chamtonau, Pavel Hraznykh and Andrew Labadzinski, will continue building the platform.
Most workforce security stacks were built for a different problem: generic phishing emails and scheduled tests.
They also run separately from the tools protecting employee devices or tracking AI usage, leaving security teams managing several disconnected products.
Noon connects directly to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and its results are built to feed into GRC platforms.
Campaign and training data is designed to support audits under frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIS2, DORA, HIPAA and GDPR, and to help meet cyber insurance requirements.

extraction.body: GHENT, Belgium, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aikido Security today announced the launch of Noon , a dedicated workforce security business that extends its protection beyond software to the people using it. AI has made sophisticated phishing, deepfakes and coordinated social engineering attacks cheaper, easier to execute and more scalable than ever before. Noon addresses these threats by bringing email protection, device protection, AI governance and phishing simulation training together in one platform. Noon's platform is being built on two acquisitions Aikido completed in September 2026: Poland-based Cyberly, founded in 2024, which brought AI-driven attack simulations and AI usage visibility, and Belgium-based Outkept, founded in 2020, which brought email security and phishing awareness training. Before the acquisitions, Cyberly protected more than 300,000 employees across 200-plus organizations, while Outkept served more than 1,000 organizations and 250,000 users across 100-plus countries. Together, Cyberly and Outkept bring established international customer relationships and a strong foundation for Noon's growth, with additional opportunities across Aikido's existing customer network. "We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security. "But companies don't just need to protect the software they build. They need to protect the people building and using it. AI is making social engineering more convincing and easier to scale, while fundamentally changing how employees work. So while novel AI attacks and agent sandboxes monopolize budget and oxygen in the security discussion, someone in finance is opening StaffSalaries2026.xls.exe. The bigger threat is still that urgent email invite to the company Christmas party asking you to RSVP via the link or lose your spot. We can’t blame humans though. Phishing has gotten good. You get an email or a calendar invite, followed by a text about that email, then a call from someone who sounds exactly like your CFO. Forty-one percent of social engineering breaches involved a channel other than email. Why? Because it works. Phone-based social engineering is about 40% more effective than email phishing. extraction.body: GHENT, Belgium, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aikido Security today announced the launch of Noon , a dedicated workforce security business that extends its protection beyond software to the people using it. AI has made sophisticated phishing, deepfakes and coordinated social engineering attacks cheaper, easier to execute and more scalable than ever before. Noon addresses these threats by bringing email protection, device protection, AI governance and phishing simulation training together in one platform. Noon's platform is being built on two acquisitions Aikido completed in September 2026: Poland-based Cyberly, founded in 2024, which brought AI-driven attack simulations and AI usage visibility, and Belgium-based Outkept, founded in 2020, which brought email security and phishing awareness training. Before the acquisitions, Cyberly protected more than 300,000 employees across 200-plus organizations, while Outkept served more than 1,000 organizations and 250,000 users across 100-plus countries. Together, Cyberly and Outkept bring established international customer relationships and a strong foundation for Noon's growth, with additional opportunities across Aikido's existing customer network. "We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security. "But companies don't just need to protect the software they build. They need to protect the people building and using it. AI is making social engineering more convincing and easier to scale, while fundamentally changing how employees work. With Noon, we're bringing the same approach to workforce security: one platform, less complexity, and protection for every employee, not just those building software." Phishing used to require research on a target, a convincing personalized message and a fake login page. AI has stripped out the time, skill and cost. Attackers can now generate targeted emails, clone a colleague's voice for a deepfake call, and run campaigns across email, SMS and chat at scale. At the same time, AI assistants and autonomous workflows have become part of everyday work, with limited visibility for security teams. "Attackers don't always need to break into software when they can simply trick the people using it. Yet the security industry has long treated software and workforce security as two separate worlds," said Alex Horlach, co-founder of Cyberly. "Aikido has already changed how companies secure their software. With Noon, we're bringing that same approach to workforce security, backed by Aikido's global reach." Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that mobile social engineering attacks, including fraudulent texts and voice calls, succeeded 40% more often than email phishing. It also found employee use of unapproved AI tools had tripled, to 45%. Most workforce security stacks were built for a different problem: generic phishing emails and scheduled tests. They also run separately from the tools protecting employee devices or tracking AI usage, leaving security teams managing several disconnected products. Noon brings employee security into one platform, replacing the separate tools many organizations piece together today: Noon connects directly to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and its results are built to feed into GRC platforms. Campaign and training data is designed to support audits under frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIS2, DORA, HIPAA and GDPR, and to help meet cyber insurance requirements. The founding teams of both companies continue at Noon. Cyberly's four co-founders, Alex Horlach, Evgeny Chamtonau, Pavel Hraznykh and Andrew Labadzinski, will continue building the platform. Outkept co-founders Simon Bauwens and Thibaut De Maerteleire now lead Noon's global MSP partnerships and email security development. Founded in Ghent, Belgium, Aikido Security is building self-securing software for modern development teams. The bigger threat is still that urgent email invite to the company Christmas party asking you to RSVP via the link or lose your spot.

We can’t blame humans though. Phishing has gotten good. By and large, phishing no longer looks like phishing. It’s no longer just princes asking for money with obvious typos (I, too, need 5 iTunes gift cards for my cat’s surgery within the next 2 hours!!!). Today’s attackers are AI-native. Phishing campaigns are sophisticated, multi-channel, and armed with enough context to make it virtually impossible to tell what’s real and what’s fake. You get an email or a calendar invite, followed by a text about that email, then a call from someone who sounds exactly like your CFO.
Forty-one percent of social engineering breaches involved a channel other than email. Why? Because it works. Phone-based social engineering is about 40% more effective than email phishing.

The proportion of employees who use AI regularly on corporate devices has tripled in one year. Every new tool, package, and agent skill introduces something else to secure.

Protecting your workforce now means understanding what people are installing, what their agents can do, and which tools can access company data. Alongside the inboxes, devices, and people you already needed to protect.
So there’s more to protect, and the attacks look more real. And it’s only getting worse. Much, much worse. AI makes attacks like these easier to create, personalize, and run at scale.

Noon brings email security, device protection, AI governance, as well as complex phishing simulations and training into one platform, covering your team everywhere they work. It’s our answer to “what about everybody else?”

We entered the workforce space because we had the same “this needs fixing ” feeling we did when we started Aikido. The bank chose the Ethereum network for its greater liquidity than other options and its existing institutional user base. JPMorgan aims to attract crypto companies looking for blockchain-based payments, as well as financial firms involved in trade settlements or tokenized assets.

In Q2 2026, JPMorgan's payments revenue rose 12%, and net interest income rose 10%, though it has not reported specific revenue from JPM Coin.

The deposit-token structure also benefits JPMorgan; when clients hold JPM Coin, the dollars remain on the bank's balance sheet as deposits. This allows the bank to continue lending those funds and earning interest, even as the cash moves to public blockchains.

JPM Coin creates a direct link to ETH because every transaction on the Ethereum mainnet incurs a gas fee, which users pay in ETH. Increased institutional activity on Ethereum could modestly increase demand for ETH to cover these fees.

While JPMorgan benefits from 24/7 transaction capabilities, access to crypto-native firms, and deposits that remain on its balance sheet, ETH gains only a large bank's endorsement and a minor stream of gas fees. passages: JPMorgan just put its dollar-backed token on Ethereum's public blockchain, and Wall Street is watching to see whether one of the world's biggest banks can finally move the needle on ETH's battered price.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction ) has officially moved its dollar-backed token, JPM Coin (JPMD), to the Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) blockchain. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain division, made JPM Coin available to select institutional clients on Ethereum’s mainnet , which is its primary public blockchain. This move brings JPM Coin to Ethereum, supplementing its previous version that was launched on Base, a more cost-effective layer-2 network developed by Coinbase Global ( NASDAQ:COIN ).

According to Kinexys, it has processed over $4 trillion in transactions since its inception, averaging about $7 billion each day. However, much of this transaction volume occurs on JPMorgan’s private Kinexys network, which operates separately from its public blockchain activities. The bank hasn’t disclosed how much of its total activity occurs on Ethereum or Base.

JPM Coin is essentially a deposit token, where each coin represents a U.S. dollar deposited in a client’s account at JPMorgan. This differs from a stablecoin, which is typically backed by a reserve pool managed by a non-bank entity.

Despite the launch, ETH did not see a price increase. ETH trades at $2,386, down 4.2% over the past week, 12.3% over the last two weeks, and 51.8% from its all-time high . So, does JPMorgan’s involvement with Ethereum provide ETH holders with a reason to be optimistic about future price increases?
Mark Wilson / Getty Images News via Getty Images

Importantly, only approved institutional clients can access JPM Coin. Retail investors are unable to buy or hold it, and all holders must have the bank’s approval. JPMorgan positions JPM Coin as a way for institutions to make payments around the clock, freeing up cash that would typically be tied up outside banking hours.

The bank chose the Ethereum network for its greater liquidity than other options and its existing institutional user base. Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs, highlighted this point, although her perspective comes from her role in promoting the product. JPMorgan aims to attract crypto companies looking for blockchain-based payments, as well as financial firms involved in trade settlements or tokenized assets.

While Kinexys represents a small portion of JPMorgan’s operations, the bank is massive, with $5 trillion in assets and revenue from consumer banking, commercial and investment banking, and asset and wealth management. In Q2 2026, JPMorgan’s payments revenue rose 12%, and net interest income rose 10%, though it has not reported specific revenue from JPM Coin.

The deposit-token structure also benefits JPMorgan; when clients hold JPM Coin, the dollars remain on the bank’s balance sheet as deposits. This allows the bank to continue lending those funds and earning interest, even as the cash moves to public blockchains.

JPM Coin creates a direct link to ETH because every transaction on the Ethereum mainnet incurs a gas fee, which users pay in ETH. Increased institutional activity on Ethereum could modestly increase demand for ETH to cover these fees.

However, each JPM Coin corresponds to one dollar. Clients only need a minimal amount of ETH for transaction fees, and JPMorgan does not require clients to hold ETH as an investment. The bank has not set a volume target for its Ethereum transactions, nor has it disclosed how many clients are utilizing the token on the mainnet.

Base serves as a useful reference point. JPM Coin has been active there since November 2025, and Base fees are also paid in ETH. However, JPMorgan has not provided any usage statistics for Base, leaving it unclear how much demand there is for ETH in that context.

The competitive landscape further constrains JPM Coin’s potential. Existing non-bank stablecoins dominate the dollar token market on Ethereum, and JPMorgan and other major banks reportedly plan a shared tokenized deposit network that could challenge both stablecoins and crypto firms. Such a network could draw bank activity toward systems they directly control.

Market trends also do not indicate a positive outlook. ETH fell by 10.4% in October leading up to October 19. On October 18, it closed 5.9% below its 20-day average and 5.6% below its 50-day average, suggesting a downward trend.

Additionally, spot Ether ETFs experienced net outflows of $103 million on October 19, the day JPM Coin launched on Ethereum. This outflow indicates that investors pulled out more money than they added. Notably, BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ:ETHA ) accounted for $95 million of that total.

In our view, JPM Coin is unlikely to significantly increase ETH’s price in the near future. While JPMorgan benefits from 24/7 transaction capabilities, access to crypto-native firms, and deposits that remain on its balance sheet, ETH gains only a large bank’s endorsement and a minor stream of gas fees. Although Ethereum burns a portion of every fee , heavy use is required to meaningfully reduce ETH’s supply.

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. Rise of cryptocurrency crimes, and how kiosks can play a role Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. States are upping regulations, oversight over crypto ATMs. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Jackson Some of the bill's language includes: Requiring licenses for all kiosk operators under the Money Transmissions Act. It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. You don't have to do that through a gas station. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. We have advocated for a waiting period for first-time customers because it gives time to stop a scam before any funds leave. CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.

passages: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station.

Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money.
That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings.
“I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally."

This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine.

The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse.
Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses.
"Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network.
Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether.
This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R).

"HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson

It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000.

North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place.

"We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL.
David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes.

"Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules."

State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger.

"I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is."
Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies.
"Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said.
WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws.

Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies.

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse. Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. "We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

Artificial intelligence (AI) is ushering in significant changes across every sector and industry, and some of the companies at the forefront have already been handsomely rewarded for their efforts, with much more to come. But with more and more companies getting in on AI, which ones are worth investing in? Perhaps it might help to take some inspiration from successful investors, such as David Tepper, the billionaire founder of the family office Appaloosa Management. Appaloosa has several prominent AI stocks in its public equity portfolio, and two of them, Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), account for about 31% of the portfolio. Are these AI stocks worth buying today? Let's find out. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Micron is one of the leaders in providing computer memory and data storage products, such as DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) chips, which are widely used in data centers. The company's shares have climbed a little more than 200% this year as its financial results have significantly improved. In the fourth quarter of its fiscal year 2026, which ended Sept. 3, Micron's revenue soared by 379% to $54.2 billion. That was more than it generated during its entire fiscal year 2025. The company's non-GAAP gross margin for the period was 87%, substantially higher than the 45.7% reported in the prior-year quarter. Micron's non-GAAP operating income was $44.6 billion at an 82.3% operating margin, versus $4 billion at 35% in the year-ago period. And Micron posted non-GAAP earnings per share of $33.42, up 1003% year over year. Micron is flying on all cylinders. But during the second quarter, Appaloosa Management reduced its stake in the stock by about 41%, likely partly to cash in some nice gains. It now accounts for 15.06% of the fund's public equity portfolio, indicating that Tepper and his team remain bullish on the company's prospects. That makes sense. Micron Technology is benefiting from a shortage of memory chips amid the massive AI build-out, which is granting the company significant pricing power. The shortage could continue at least through 2028, according to some projections, and Micron sees significant demand through that year. Micron's incredible sales and earnings growth will eventually slow and normalize. But note that the market is arguably already factoring that in. The company is trading at just 7x forward earnings, versus an average of 19.7x for information technology stocks. At current levels, Micron's shares remain attractive. Amazon was the largest holding in Appaloosa Management's public equity portfolio as of the second quarter, accounting for almost 16% of the portfolio. What's more, during the period, Tepper and his team increased their stake in the conglomerate by about 15.7%. That was, in my view, a good move. Amazon is performing well. Second-quarter revenue jumped 20% year over year to $200.6 billion, while the company's net earnings per share came in at $5.75, up 242% from the year-ago period (in fairness, Amazon's EPS included a positive impact from equity investments). Amazon's cloud business , Amazon Web Services, performed particularly well. It posted net sales of $42.2 billion, up 37% year over year. The company's AI business is playing a key role here, and there is more where that came from. Amazon is guiding for $220 billion in capex this year, up from its previous projection of $200 billion (the increase was partly due to higher memory prices). That's a significant sum, but Amazon appears to be in a strong position to monetize its investments over the medium term. The company already has cloud demand visibility through 2028, for instance. Even beyond its cloud business, though, Amazon has attractive growth opportunities. The company's high-margin advertising segment continues to grow at a good clip, while it is looking to make productivity and margin gains within its largest segment by sales -- e-commerce -- notably through AI-powered initiatives. Amazon has performed more or less in line with broader equities this year, and over the next five years, the company is well-positioned to deliver strong returns. Artificial intelligence (AI) is ushering in significant changes across every sector and industry, and some of the companies at the forefront have already been handsomely rewarded for their efforts, with much more to come. But with more and more companies getting in on AI, which ones are worth investing in?

Perhaps it might help to take some inspiration from successful investors, such as David Tepper, the billionaire founder of the family office Appaloosa Management. Appaloosa has several prominent AI stocks in its public equity portfolio, and two of them, Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), account for about 31% of the portfolio. Are these AI stocks worth buying today? Let's find out.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Micron is one of the leaders in providing computer memory and data storage products, such as DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) chips, which are widely used in data centers. The company's shares have climbed a little more than 200% this year as its financial results have significantly improved. In the fourth quarter of its fiscal year 2026, which ended Sept. 3, Micron's revenue soared by 379% to $54.2 billion. That was more than it generated during its entire fiscal year 2025.

The company's non-GAAP gross margin for the period was 87%, substantially higher than the 45.7% reported in the prior-year quarter. Micron's non-GAAP operating income was $44.6 billion at an 82.3% operating margin, versus $4 billion at 35% in the year-ago period.

And Micron posted non-GAAP earnings per share of $33.42, up 1003% year over year. Micron is flying on all cylinders. But during the second quarter, Appaloosa Management reduced its stake in the stock by about 41%, likely partly to cash in some nice gains. It now accounts for 15.06% of the fund's public equity portfolio, indicating that Tepper and his team remain bullish on the company's prospects.

That makes sense. Micron Technology is benefiting from a shortage of memory chips amid the massive AI build-out, which is granting the company significant pricing power. The shortage could continue at least through 2028, according to some projections, and Micron sees significant demand through that year.

Micron's incredible sales and earnings growth will eventually slow and normalize. But note that the market is arguably already factoring that in. The company is trading at just 7x forward earnings, versus an average of 19.7x for information technology stocks. At current levels, Micron's shares remain attractive.

Amazon was the largest holding in Appaloosa Management's public equity portfolio as of the second quarter, accounting for almost 16% of the portfolio. What's more, during the period, Tepper and his team increased their stake in the conglomerate by about 15.7%. That was, in my view, a good move.

Amazon is performing well. Second-quarter revenue jumped 20% year over year to $200.6 billion, while the company's net earnings per share came in at $5.75, up 242% from the year-ago period (in fairness, Amazon's EPS included a positive impact from equity investments).

Amazon's cloud business , Amazon Web Services, performed particularly well. It posted net sales of $42.2 billion, up 37% year over year. The company's AI business is playing a key role here, and there is more where that came from. Amazon is guiding for $220 billion in capex this year, up from its previous projection of $200 billion (the increase was partly due to higher memory prices).

That's a significant sum, but Amazon appears to be in a strong position to monetize its investments over the medium term. The company already has cloud demand visibility through 2028, for instance. Even beyond its cloud business, though, Amazon has attractive growth opportunities.

The company's high-margin advertising segment continues to grow at a good clip, while it is looking to make productivity and margin gains within its largest segment by sales -- e-commerce -- notably through AI-powered initiatives. Amazon has performed more or less in line with broader equities this year, and over the next five years, the company is well-positioned to deliver strong returns.
Before you buy stock in Micron Technology, consider this:

The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Micron Technology wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $380,363 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,315,732 !*

Built from the ground up with AI, Juicebox understands the types of candidates recruiters are looking for in the same way a person does. It can interpret nuanced context around roles and regions, verify that candidate information is still accurate, and learn from a team's prior outreach and hiring decisions so results consistently reflect the company's talent bar. MIAMI , Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nucleus Research's 2026 Full-Suite Talent Acquisition Technology Value Matrix examines how organizations are using integrated HCM technology to improve recruiting efficiency, accelerate hiring, and manage growing talent acquisition demands without proportional increases in administrative resources. Fragmented recruiting systems and manual processes continue to create operational challenges for organizations seeking to scale hiring. Full-suite HCM platforms address these challenges by connecting recruiting and onboarding with workforce planning, compensation, internal mobility, and employee referrals. Centralized candidate and employee data can reduce integration requirements, improve process coordination, and support more efficient use of recruiting resources. Agentic AI is emerging as a significant area of investment, with vendors developing multi-agent frameworks to automate candidate sourcing, pre-screening, interview scheduling, and recruiting workflows. These capabilities offer opportunities to reduce repetitive work and expand recruiter capacity while maintaining human oversight. "Talent acquisition ROI depends on how effectively organizations can scale recruiting activity while reducing the administrative effort behind each hire," said Evelyn McMullen , Research Director at Nucleus Research . "Connecting recruiting with broader workforce data and applying AI across the hiring lifecycle can help organizations improve productivity, accelerate hiring processes, and make better use of existing talent." Candidate experience is also shaping product development. Self-scheduling and multichannel conversational AI are becoming standard capabilities as vendors address interview coordination bottlenecks and candidate drop-off. Investments in applicant re-engagement, database mining, and predictive pipeline recommendations are helping recruiting teams identify and prioritize potential candidates. As agentic capabilities mature, data privacy, governance, and explainability remain important considerations. Full-suite providers are extending automation across recruiting, onboarding, and workforce management, creating additional opportunities for organizations to improve hiring efficiency through connected processes. Leaders in the Value Matrix excel in both functionality and usability, offering consolidated integration that delivers strong returns and supports adoption at scale. Leaders in this year's Value Matrix are Cegid, HiBob, Infor, Oracle, and Paycor. Experts offer deep, specialized integration functionality suited to complex and technical requirements. Experts in this year's Value Matrix are Dayforce, Personio, SAP SuccessFactors, and Workday. Accelerators focus on usability and ease of deployment, delivering integration that enables quick adoption. This year's Accelerators are BambooHR, isolved, and Paychex Flex. Nucleus Research is the recognized global leader in ROI technology research. Its AI agents can then handle outreach and follow-ups automatically, while giving teams real-time insights into the talent market. Later that afternoon, Penn State DuBois Wildlife Technology faculty and alumni led a forest management-focused hike at Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake for a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania through the American Hardwood Export Council (AHEC). DuBOIS, Pa. — Students, faculty and alumni from Penn State DuBois' Wildlife Technology program participated in two educational hikes on Oct. 4 as part of the annual Walk in Penn's Woods initiative, sharing their knowledge of tree identification, forest management and conservation with local community members and international visitors.

During the morning hike at Bilger's Rocks, first-year Wildlife Technology students collaborated with staff from the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources Bureau of Forestry to provide an educational experience focused on tree identification. The hike took place at Bilger's Rocks, which recently became part of Moshannon State Forest, and gave participants an opportunity to learn about the region's trees and other plant species.

As part of their coursework, Wildlife Technology students learn to identify more than 100 species of trees, shrubs and vines, developing skills essential to careers in wildlife and natural resource management. Participating in the public hike allowed the students to apply that knowledge outside the classroom while sharing what they have learned with community members.
“Experiences like Walk in Penn's Woods give our students an opportunity to take what they're learning in the classroom and apply it in a real-world setting.”
Mike Eckley , assistant teaching professor in forestry, Penn State DuBois

"Experiences like Walk in Penn's Woods give our students an opportunity to take what they're learning in the classroom and apply it in a real-world setting," Mike Eckley, assistant teaching professor in forestry at Penn State DuBois said. "They're not only strengthening their knowledge of the natural environment, but also developing the communication and professional skills they'll need as the next generation of wildlife and natural resource managers."

Later that afternoon, Penn State DuBois Wildlife Technology faculty and alumni led a forest management-focused hike at Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake for a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania through the American Hardwood Export Council (AHEC).

The journalists were visiting Pennsylvania as part of the production of "Forested Future," a film highlighting the sustainability, management and stewardship of American hardwood forests. Their visit to Treasure Lake provided an opportunity to showcase regional forest management practices, wildlife habitat improvements and partnerships supporting responsible forestry.

Eckley led the hike alongside recent Penn State graduate Elizabeth Bruner, who now works for the Pennsylvania Game Commission. Together, they discussed differences between public and private land management and explained how forestry practices contribute to healthy forest ecosystems.

Penn State alumna Elizabeth Bruner shares her knowledge during a hike at the Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake, in Clearfield County. The hike was attended by a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania. Credit: Penn State . Creative Commons

The hike highlighted recently completed forestry practices at Community Woodlands, where partnerships with Domtar Paper Company, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Ruffed Grouse Society and Audubon Mid-Atlantic have supported forest management and conservation efforts.

Through these partnerships, the project has supported timber stand improvement, wildlife habitat creation and invasive species removal. Eckley has also involved Penn State fisheries, wildlife and forestry students in the work, providing hands-on opportunities to learn about forest management and conservation.

The forest management project has also included the salvage harvesting of two American chestnut trees from the property. The Allegheny Hardwood Utilization Group, whose executive director, Amy Shields, helped arrange the journalists' visit, coordinated kiln drying of the lumber through Forcey Lumber in Woodland. Shields also serves on the Wildlife Technology program's advisory board and has supported student professional development through summer internship opportunities.
Eckley plans to work with Pennsylvania forest and wood products organizations to create commemorative pieces from the lumber in recognition of America's 250th anniversary.

A special preliminary showing of "Forested Future," a video production featuring Pennsylvania forests, local footage and interviews with natural resource professionals, is being planned for later this winter at Penn State DuBois. Students, faculty, staff and community members will be invited to attend, with additional details to be announced as plans are finalized.

Together, the two hikes demonstrated how Penn State DuBois' Wildlife Technology program connects classroom learning with practical experience while supporting conservation education and responsible forest management. Through partnerships with government agencies, industry professionals and conservation organizations, the program continues to provide students with opportunities to develop their skills, engage with the community and contribute to the stewardship of Pennsylvania's natural resources.

passages: Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak.

Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.
Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies .
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable.
They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways.

In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.
It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task.
That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

sources.title: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop - CNBC
passages: Apple announced a product launch event on Oct.
28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles."
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall.
He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.

It will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.
Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors.
Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500.
In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones.
But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024.
Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.

facts.text: (Bloomberg) -- Apple Inc. on Monday confirmed that it's holding a product launch event on Oct.
28, where the company is planning to debut its first touch-screen MacBook.
The event, which will take place in Los Angeles, is dubbed "Pro and tell," a nod to the MacBook Pro update.
Apple will also introduce a new low-end MacBook Pro with an M6 chip, a refreshed iMac and a revamped iPad mini with a sharper screen, Bloomberg News has reported.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The new touch MacBooks are expected to include a Dynamic Island interface — like on the iPhone — as well as a sharper display that uses OLED technology.
Apple announced a product launch event on Oct.
28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles."
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall.
He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.

It will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.
Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors.
Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500.
In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones.
But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024.
Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.

sources.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content - TechCrunch
passages: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

passages: Spotify may not be a dedicated podcast platform, but it is launching a big new feature in podcast memberships that let you support your favorite shows in exchange for added perks.
Available starting today, Spotify podcast memberships work similarly to Patreon and other membership programs.
Hosts can create support tiers with a monthly fee that deliver perks to their audience and, in turn, support the show.
Spotify says examples of what creators can provide in these memberships include “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads, early access, access to a show’s archive” and more.
Multiple tiers can be created and pricing is customizable.

Shows launching membership programs today include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society, Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows across the YMH Studios network.
