Spotify is enabling podcast creators to earn more money through the platform by providing their fans with a way to pay to access exclusive content.

Spotify is providing podcasters with tools to analyze and build their Memberships audience, including targeted promotions and free trial offers, alongside community engagement features like member badges, welcome clips, and more.

Spotify is also making it easy for podcasters who manage their subscriptions on other services to try Memberships, allowing them to bring their paywalled content to Spotify via its Open Access feature.

First announced in May, the new Memberships subscription feature is starting to roll out in 34 regions today, allowing podcasters to offer perks including additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads behind a paywall.
Podcast creators can set their pricing options and bundle benefits across multiple subscription tiers, and keep 90 percent of membership revenue.

coreStoryFacts.text: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

story.title: Spotify’s new podcast memberships let you pay for extra perks

facts.text: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

Spotify may not be a dedicated podcast platform, but it is launching a big new feature in podcast memberships that let you support your favorite shows in exchange for added perks.
Available starting today, Spotify podcast memberships work similarly to Patreon and other membership programs.
Hosts can create support tiers with a monthly fee that deliver perks to their audience and, in turn, support the show.
Spotify says examples of what creators can provide in these memberships include “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads, early access, access to a show’s archive” and more.
Multiple tiers can be created and pricing is customizable.

Shows launching membership programs today include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society, Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows across the YMH Studios network.
Users can find Memberships on a podcast’s Spotify page, with the ability to subscribe, pay, and access the exclusive benefits “in just a few taps,” according to Spotify.

That makes this more like a Patreon-style membership system in which fans can choose to give additional support to their favorite creators, and is distinct from the podcast subscription feature that Spotify introduced in 2021.
Podcasters can utilize Memberships alongside other Spotify revenue streams, including ads and the Spotify Partner Program.
To qualify for Memberships, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, and have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and three published episodes.
Spotify is enabling podcast creators to earn more money through the platform by providing their fans with a way to pay to access exclusive content.

Spotify is providing podcasters with tools to analyze and build their Memberships audience, including targeted promotions and free trial offers, alongside community engagement features like member badges, welcome clips, and more.

Spotify is also making it easy for podcasters who manage their subscriptions on other services to try Memberships, allowing them to bring their paywalled content to Spotify via its Open Access feature.

First announced in May, the new Memberships subscription feature is starting to roll out in 34 regions today, allowing podcasters to offer perks including additional content, early access, bonus episodes, and reduced ads behind a paywall.
Podcast creators can set their pricing options and bundle benefits across multiple subscription tiers, and keep 90 percent of membership revenue.

28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles."

Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.

facts.text: Apple announced a product launch event on Oct.
28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles."
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall.
He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.

It will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.
Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.
Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors.
Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500.
In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones.
But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024.
Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.
Apple has scheduled a product launch event for October 28, fuelling speculation that the company could unveil new Mac computers, including its first touchscreen laptop.

The invitation, sent to media and analysts on Monday, describes an “Apple Experience in Los Angeles” and carries the tagline “Pro and tell”, hinting at a possible focus on premium devices and next-generation chips.

The upcoming event follows Apple's recent efforts to strengthen its Mac lineup.

sources.title: TikTok employees said they knew about child safety issues, but execs failed to act
passages: Despite flagging that “minor safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively,” Han said that TikTok failed to warn parents of the potential dangers of their child using the platform.
TikTok was repeatedly warned by its own staffers about risks its platform posed to child safety, according to court records obtained by NPR.

The publication reports that employees were frustrated over TikTok executives failing to appropriately act on concerns they raised, including minors bypassing age-restricted content, and appearing in “transactional sexual content” the company could financially benefit from.

One deposition from Reagen Maher, who held senior safety and investigations positions between 2021 and 2024, described flagging the prevalence of “transactional sexual content” to then-TikTok CEO V Pappas, regarding minors stripping on TikTok’s Live feature in exchange for “gifts” that can be converted into real currency.

There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I’m hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions.” Another deposition from TikTok’s former head of safety Eric Han says he was concerned about harmful algorithm “rabbit holes” in 2020, describing them as having a “real contagion effect” regarding “suicidal ideation and behavior” in an internal TikTok report.

The publication reports that employees were frustrated over TikTok executives failing to appropriately act on concerns they raised, including minors bypassing age-restricted content, and appearing in “transactional sexual content” the company could financially benefit from. The previously unreported depositions of TikTok staffers were filed in federal court in March, and connected to a multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 that brings together hundreds of lawsuits alleging that TikTok, Meta, Snap, and Google knew that they social media platforms are harmful to children, and failed to disclose those risks. One deposition from Reagen Maher, who held senior safety and investigations positions between 2021 and 2024, described flagging the prevalence of “transactional sexual content” to then-TikTok CEO V Pappas, regarding minors stripping on TikTok’s Live feature in exchange for “gifts” that can be converted into real currency. Forbes reported on the issue in 2022, and Maher said the company was already aware of the sexual exploitation concerns before the article was published. “I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn’t think the harms are severe enough,” Maher said in an excerpt from an internal chat with a colleague. “Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I’m hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions.” Another deposition from TikTok’s former head of safety Eric Han says he was concerned about harmful algorithm “rabbit holes” in 2020, describing them as having a “real contagion effect” regarding “suicidal ideation and behavior” in an internal TikTok report. Despite flagging that “minor safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively,” Han said that TikTok failed to warn parents of the potential dangers of their child using the platform.

The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said . The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. China’s foreign ministry told Reuters that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies, with Mao Ning saying China “consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues.” The U.S. ban framed DeepSeek as a national security risk by alleging that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including that DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC and that the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure.

The order also barred DeepSeek from future procurements and extended the restriction beyond DeepSeek itself to third-party products and services developed using its implementations, raising questions about software provenance and supply-chain compliance.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove products developed by Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) startup DeepSeek from their information technology systems and barred them from procuring such products, according to a federal notice released Monday.

The order, detailed in a notice scheduled to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, applies to information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. and its affiliated entities.
The restrictions also cover third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.

The department said the order was issued under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 following a review of a recommendation by the Federal Acquisition Security Council and related evidence.
The order applies to federal civilian agency IT systems and procurements, rather than imposing a general ban on the use of DeepSeek products by private businesses or individuals in the United States.

The South Korean government also moved to restrict the use of DeepSeek in February 2025, with its foreign, trade and defense ministries blocking access to the Chinese AI service on government computers amid concerns over user data collection and potential information leaks.

extraction.body: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions. The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said . The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models. China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added. The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems. Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week . The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares. The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report. In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, and it also blocked civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The order, dating back to late July, applied to federal civilian agencies including the departments of the Treasury, State and Justice, while excluding the Department of Defense. The DHS notice in the Federal Register alleged that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including concerns that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data. Mao Ning, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson, said China would “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked about the U.S. ban at a regular press conference. The U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China, with AI expected to be on the agenda. The DHS order warned that using DeepSeek’s AI models could result in sensitive government information being transferred to China, potentially exposing intelligence concerning American citizens and government programmes. The DHS also raised concerns that the models could contain malware or other security weaknesses, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek’s iOS application. The notice described a compliance requirement that executive agencies can request exemptions, including extensions to the compliance deadline, by submitting written justifications to the DHS within 60 days of the order’s issuance. The Department of Homeland Security said the use of DeepSeek AI tools “could lead to the transfer of sensitive data to (China) if used by U.S. government employees or contractors,” and it warned that DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. The U.S. government said the directive applies to all products from the Chinese AI leader, as well as third-party services using its models, while the order does not establish a global ban on Chinese models or prevent independent researchers from studying their capabilities. China’s foreign ministry told Reuters that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies, with Mao Ning saying China “consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues.” The U.S. ban framed DeepSeek as a national security risk by alleging that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including that DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC and that the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure. The order also barred DeepSeek from future procurements and extended the restriction beyond DeepSeek itself to third-party products and services developed using its implementations, raising questions about software provenance and supply-chain compliance. The DHS order did not immediately prompt a response from DeepSeek, and the order’s scope remained limited to federal civilian agencies’ information technology systems and procurement activities rather than a general prohibition on private companies or individual users. facts.text: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
“We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.

Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week .
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China.
DHS orders removal of DeepSeek AI from federal civilian agencies and bans new contracts.
Order cites security concerns and threat vectors; applies to affiliates and third-party services using DeepSeek.

China’s foreign ministry told Reuters that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies, with Mao Ning saying China “consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues.” The U.S. ban framed DeepSeek as a national security risk by alleging that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors,” including that DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC and that the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure.

The DHS order required agencies to remove versions put into place prior to the ban and to check that they had not already been compromised, while also warning organizations to monitor the flow of traffic in and out of the agency and implement enhanced logging and controls for relevant systems.

The order also barred DeepSeek from future procurements and extended the restriction beyond DeepSeek itself to third-party products and services developed using its implementations, raising questions about software provenance and supply-chain compliance.

For starters, if you want to mount the HomeView, it’ll run you up to $130, depending on the mount you choose. Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t. If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home. Plus, if you want seamless compatibility between devices like your iPhone and your smart home hub, this is the best way to do it. Apple's joined the smart home category with the new HomeView, but Amazon isn't moving out anytime soon.
Article updated on October 16, 2026, 11:25 am EDT

No smart home is complete without a hub to manage it, and for a long time, Amazon’s Echo line or Google’s home system was the go-to choice. Apple has finally entered the smart home market with the launch of the HomeView , a direct competitor to the aforementioned brands, and we’ve recently gone hands-on with it.
Also: Apple’s $299 HomeView smart hub is here: 8 highlights, including the wall model

The new device resembles an iPad and is a control center for all your connected smart home devices, including any smart speakers, video doorbells, or smart locks — all of which Apple also announced. So who’s it really for, and how does it compare to popular options like Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) from 2025? Here’s what you should know before making that preorder.

If you’re a die-hard Apple user who’s been waiting for Apple’s new home products, this launch is for you. The HomeView expands Apple’s traditional ecosystem, taking it one step further by bringing many of your favorite Apple features to a smart home hub. It syncs Siri, creates unique profiles for members of your family, tracks locations with FindMy, delivers Intercom messages, and more.
Also: I saw Apple’s HomeView, HomePod Mini 2, and Apple TV 4K – and I’m sold on one

However, chances are, if you’re eyeing the HomeView for your smart home hub, you’re aware there may be extra costs associated with it. For starters, if you want to mount the HomeView, it’ll run you up to $130, depending on the mount you choose. Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t. If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home.

If Siri is your go-to pocket companion, there’s no doubt that you’ll want to add Siri to your home’s hub. Plus, if you want seamless compatibility between devices like your iPhone and your smart home hub, this is the best way to do it. You’ll be able to take FaceTime calls, check locations, and more, as you would on your iPhone, right from Apple’s HomeView.

If you want a smart hub, but don’t want to spend $299 (or more), Amazon’s Echo Show 8 is an all-around better choice. It’s already cheaper, plus it’s not uncommon to see the device discounted even further depending on the time of year. It was just on sale during Prime Day, and it has sold for as low as $125. That’s a great deal on a smart home hub that seamlessly integrates with Alexa and Echo devices, as well as security systems like Ring. If you’re evaluating primarily on price, the Echo Show 8 wins hands-down.

Smart hubs are often the starting point to expand one’s home’s technological offerings. If you foresee yourself purchasing more types of compatible smart accessories along the way, I also have to pay a nod to Alexa’s Echo Show 8 (and family). Amazon’s Echo lineup includes speakers, alarm clocks, displays, lights, and truly takes a well-rounded, robust approach to elevating your home.

Plus, Echo devices and the Alexa system are compatible with other smart devices, like various plugs, sensors, and monitors. Eventually, Apple’s products will likely share wider compatibility, but as it stands right now, the Echo device offerings offer numerous arrangements for many different needs, and the compatibility with Alexa makes it that much better.
Also: Renting? These 2 new Apple smart home devices are worth your money (and these 5 are not)

And if you already have several Alexa-compatible devices? It makes sense to continue with items like the Echo Show 8. And if the Echo Show 8 isn’t your jam — that’s OK. Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes.

Apple’s HomeKit will likely catch up in its compatibility offerings with other smart home products on the market, but if you need max compatibility and variety right now, Amazon and its suite of Echo Show offerings are where it’s at.

I’m a big fan of using tech until it’s no longer functioning (or it no longer meets my needs). I have two Alexa speakers and an Echo Show 5 in my home, and my security sensors and cameras are set up through Ring, which is already compatible with my Amazon devices.

But I’m no stranger to Apple’s ecosystem, either. I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper. But since I already have a smart home hub and security setup I’m happy with, I see no reason to spend more money on an all new setup.
Also: How Apple’s video doorbell privacy compares to Ring, Wyze, and Blink

If you’re a first-time smart home hub buyer, or you’re really set on having a seamless Apple ecosystem, it makes sense. But my general consensus is that Amazon and Google have spent years in the smart home market building and refining great products at better price points than Apple — especially if you find them on sale. You can also bet Apple’s Home lineup won’t be discounted very often, much like the rest of Apple’s products.

sources.title: I saw Apple's HomeView early — 7 things you need to know about the new smart home display - Tom's Guide
passages: I got an early look at Apple's new $299 smart home display ahead of its official announcement, and what struck is that HomeView doesn't feel like an iPad attached to a speaker or an oversized Apple Watch.

Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.”
Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home.
You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously.
The more I saw of HomeView, the more I realized Apple is serious about giving its smart home ecosystem something it's been missing all along: a centerpiece.
When it comes to controlling smart home devices, an optimally-placed, wall-mounted control center tends to be a preferred interface.
Apple has spent years making products for just about every part of our lives.
There's an iPhone in our pockets, an Apple Watch on our wrists, AirPods in our ears, Macs on our desks and an Apple TV in our living rooms.
But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment.
The tabletop HomeView comes with a speaker base featuring a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, along with two full-range drivers in the tilting display itself.
Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups.

Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life.
No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones.
Between FaceTime, recipes, music, photos and personalized information, there's plenty here for someone who hasn't invested much in smart home technology.
And for those who have, HomeView could be the missing link that brings everything together.
Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces.
Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly.
That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device.
HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits.
That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered.
That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.
Unlock the vast world of Apple news straight to your inbox.
Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions.
Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events.
Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message.
Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone.
HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls.
But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be.

Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.” Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life. Between its personalized interface, surprisingly clever cooking features and new Siri AI capabilities, I came away from the demonstration with a breakdown of these seven features that stand out most. Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly. That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device. Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events. We've heard plenty about how Apple is making Siri smarter with personal context, but Apple's demonstration gave me a more tangible example of what that means. Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message. Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone. The same intelligence can help with calendar requests, questions about everyday topics and other tasks that would typically send you reaching for your phone. Apple says Siri requests are processed on HomeView’s A18 processor, while relevant personal context is retrieved from your iPhone (15 Pro or newer supporting Apple Intelligence.) It's an interesting approach because your iPhone essentially remains the keeper of your personal information, even when you're interacting with another device, but only you can request the use of personal context. Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces. There are clock faces, modular layouts with widgets, a moving Flow face that reminded me of a lava lamp and even an animated Snoopy face. The Photos face is especially appealing. You can display images of specific people, places or albums, including shared albums, and have them rotate throughout the day. Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups. There are still some important questions, particularly around how reliably Siri AI handles personal context and how limiting the lack of a traditional App Store in “HomeView Software” might be. But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be. Apple's joined the smart home category with the new HomeView, but Amazon isn't moving out anytime soon. Article updated on October 16, 2026, 11:25 am EDT No smart home is complete without a hub to manage it, and for a long time, Amazon’s Echo line or Google’s home system was the go-to choice. Apple has finally entered the smart home market with the launch of the HomeView , a direct competitor to the aforementioned brands, and we’ve recently gone hands-on with it. Also: Apple’s $299 HomeView smart hub is here: 8 highlights, including the wall model The new device resembles an iPad and is a control center for all your connected smart home devices, including any smart speakers, video doorbells, or smart locks — all of which Apple also announced. So who’s it really for, and how does it compare to popular options like Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) from 2025? Here’s what you should know before making that preorder. If you’re a die-hard Apple user who’s been waiting for Apple’s new home products, this launch is for you. The HomeView expands Apple’s traditional ecosystem, taking it one step further by bringing many of your favorite Apple features to a smart home hub. It syncs Siri, creates unique profiles for members of your family, tracks locations with FindMy, delivers Intercom messages, and more. Also: I saw Apple’s HomeView, HomePod Mini 2, and Apple TV 4K – and I’m sold on one However, chances are, if you’re eyeing the HomeView for your smart home hub, you’re aware there may be extra costs associated with it. For starters, if you want to mount the HomeView, it’ll run you up to $130, depending on the mount you choose. Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t. If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home. If Siri is your go-to pocket companion, there’s no doubt that you’ll want to add Siri to your home’s hub. Plus, if you want seamless compatibility between devices like your iPhone and your smart home hub, this is the best way to do it. You’ll be able to take FaceTime calls, check locations, and more, as you would on your iPhone, right from Apple’s HomeView. If you want a smart hub, but don’t want to spend $299 (or more), Amazon’s Echo Show 8 is an all-around better choice. It’s already cheaper, plus it’s not uncommon to see the device discounted even further depending on the time of year. It was just on sale during Prime Day, and it has sold for as low as $125. That’s a great deal on a smart home hub that seamlessly integrates with Alexa and Echo devices, as well as security systems like Ring. If you’re evaluating primarily on price, the Echo Show 8 wins hands-down. Smart hubs are often the starting point to expand one’s home’s technological offerings. If you foresee yourself purchasing more types of compatible smart accessories along the way, I also have to pay a nod to Alexa’s Echo Show 8 (and family). Amazon’s Echo lineup includes speakers, alarm clocks, displays, lights, and truly takes a well-rounded, robust approach to elevating your home. Plus, Echo devices and the Alexa system are compatible with other smart devices, like various plugs, sensors, and monitors. Eventually, Apple’s products will likely share wider compatibility, but as it stands right now, the Echo device offerings offer numerous arrangements for many different needs, and the compatibility with Alexa makes it that much better. Also: Renting? These 2 new Apple smart home devices are worth your money (and these 5 are not) And if you already have several Alexa-compatible devices? It makes sense to continue with items like the Echo Show 8. And if the Echo Show 8 isn’t your jam — that’s OK. Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes. Apple’s HomeKit will likely catch up in its compatibility offerings with other smart home products on the market, but if you need max compatibility and variety right now, Amazon and its suite of Echo Show offerings are where it’s at. I’m a big fan of using tech until it’s no longer functioning (or it no longer meets my needs). I have two Alexa speakers and an Echo Show 5 in my home, and my security sensors and cameras are set up through Ring, which is already compatible with my Amazon devices. But I’m no stranger to Apple’s ecosystem, either. I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper. But since I already have a smart home hub and security setup I’m happy with, I see no reason to spend more money on an all new setup. Also: How Apple’s video doorbell privacy compares to Ring, Wyze, and Blink If you’re a first-time smart home hub buyer, or you’re really set on having a seamless Apple ecosystem, it makes sense. But my general consensus is that Amazon and Google have spent years in the smart home market building and refining great products at better price points than Apple — especially if you find them on sale. You can also bet Apple’s Home lineup won’t be discounted very often, much like the rest of Apple’s products. Amazon’s Echo lineup includes speakers, alarm clocks, displays, lights, and truly takes a well-rounded, robust approach to elevating your home.

Plus, Echo devices and the Alexa system are compatible with other smart devices, like various plugs, sensors, and monitors. Eventually, Apple’s products will likely share wider compatibility, but as it stands right now, the Echo device offerings offer numerous arrangements for many different needs, and the compatibility with Alexa makes it that much better.
Also: Renting? These 2 new Apple smart home devices are worth your money (and these 5 are not)

And if you already have several Alexa-compatible devices? It makes sense to continue with items like the Echo Show 8. And if the Echo Show 8 isn’t your jam — that’s OK. Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes.

Apple’s HomeKit will likely catch up in its compatibility offerings with other smart home products on the market, but if you need max compatibility and variety right now, Amazon and its suite of Echo Show offerings are where it’s at.

I’m a big fan of using tech until it’s no longer functioning (or it no longer meets my needs). I have two Alexa speakers and an Echo Show 5 in my home, and my security sensors and cameras are set up through Ring, which is already compatible with my Amazon devices.

But I’m no stranger to Apple’s ecosystem, either. I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper. But since I already have a smart home hub and security setup I’m happy with, I see no reason to spend more money on an all new setup.
Also: How Apple’s video doorbell privacy compares to Ring, Wyze, and Blink

If you’re a first-time smart home hub buyer, or you’re really set on having a seamless Apple ecosystem, it makes sense. But my general consensus is that Amazon and Google have spent years in the smart home market building and refining great products at better price points than Apple — especially if you find them on sale. You can also bet Apple’s Home lineup won’t be discounted very often, much like the rest of Apple’s products.

Between its personalized interface, surprisingly clever cooking features and new Siri AI capabilities, I came away from the demonstration with a breakdown of these seven features that stand out most. Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly. That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device. Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events. We've heard plenty about how Apple is making Siri smarter with personal context, but Apple's demonstration gave me a more tangible example of what that means. Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message. Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone. The same intelligence can help with calendar requests, questions about everyday topics and other tasks that would typically send you reaching for your phone. Apple says Siri requests are processed on HomeView’s A18 processor, while relevant personal context is retrieved from your iPhone (15 Pro or newer supporting Apple Intelligence.) It's an interesting approach because your iPhone essentially remains the keeper of your personal information, even when you're interacting with another device, but only you can request the use of personal context. When I’ve used Amazon’s smart displays in the past, it's been, primarily, to follow recipes. Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions. You can AirDrop a recipe from your iPhone or search for one directly using Safari, or using personal context, ask for a recipe sent to you in iMessage or Mail to be surfaced. Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces. There are clock faces, modular layouts with widgets, a moving Flow face that reminded me of a lava lamp and even an animated Snoopy face. The Photos face is especially appealing. You can display images of specific people, places or albums, including shared albums, and have them rotate throughout the day. As is the case for iPhone wallpapers, Portrait photos look particularly dynamic. HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits. That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered. That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house. HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls. I can see this being particularly convenient in a kitchen, where you might want to chat with someone while preparing dinner, or in a living room where several family members want to join the same call. You can also hand off FaceTime calls from your other Apple devices. No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones. Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home. You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously. It's also teaming up with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric on an entirely new lineup of products called the Apple Home Collection. When it comes to controlling smart home devices, an optimally-placed, wall-mounted control center tends to be a preferred interface. That’s why Apple is introducing two versions of HomeView hardware at the same price. The tabletop HomeView comes with a speaker base featuring a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, along with two full-range drivers in the tilting display itself. Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups. The wall-mounted model, meanwhile, has audio tuned for its placement and is particularly well-suited for smart home controls. It will offer three mounting options, including two in-wall solutions developed with Schneider Electric. The more I saw of HomeView, the more I realized Apple is serious about giving its smart home ecosystem something it's been missing all along: a centerpiece. Between FaceTime, recipes, music, photos and personalized information, there's plenty here for someone who hasn't invested much in smart home technology. And for those who have, HomeView could be the missing link that brings everything together. There are still some important questions, particularly around how reliably Siri AI handles personal context and how limiting the lack of a traditional App Store in “HomeView Software” might be. But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be. Apple has spent years finding its way into nearly every corner of our lives. With HomeView, it might have finally figured out how to make the home itself feel like an Apple product. extraction.body: To enable cookies, follow the instructions for your browser below. There is a specific issue with the Facebook in-app browser intermittently making requests to websites without cookies that had previously been set. This appears to be a defect in the browser which should be addressed soon. The simplest approach to avoid this problem is to continue to use the Facebook app but not use the in-app browser. This can be done through the following steps: 1. Open the settings menu by clicking the hamburger menu in the top right 2. Choose “App Settings” from the menu 3. Turn on the option “Links Open Externally” (This will use the device’s default browser) Enabling Cookies in Internet Explorer 7, 8 & 9 1. Open the Internet Browser 2. Click Tools > Internet Options > Privacy > Advanced 3. Check Override automatic cookie handling 4. For First-party Cookies and Third-party Cookies click Accept 5. Click OK and OK Enabling Cookies in Firefox 1. Open the Firefox browser 2. Click Tools > Options > Privacy > Use custom settings for history 3. Check Accept cookies from sites 4. Check Accept third party cookies 5. Select Keep until: they expire 6. Click OK Enabling Cookies in Google Chrome 1. Open the Google Chrome browser 2. Click Tools > Options > Privacy Options > Under the Hood > Content Settings 3. Check Allow local data to be set 4. Uncheck Block third-party cookies from being set 5. Uncheck Clear cookies 6. Close all Enabling Cookies in Mobile Safari (iPhone, iPad) 1. Go to the Home screen by pressing the Home button or by unlocking your phone/iPad 2. Select the Settings icon. 3. Select Safari from the settings menu. 4. Select ‘accept cookies’ from the safari menu. 5. Select ‘from visited’ from the accept cookies menu. 6. Press the home button to return the the iPhone home screen. 7. Select the Safari icon to return to Safari. 8. Before the cookie settings change will take effect, Safari must restart. To restart Safari press and hold the Home button (for around five seconds) until the iPhone/iPad display goes blank and the home screen appears. 9. Select the Safari icon to return to Safari.

So who’s it really for, and how does it compare to popular options like Amazon’s Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) from 2025?
Here’s what you should know before making that preorder.
It’s already cheaper, plus it’s not uncommon to see the device discounted even further depending on the time of year.
It was just on sale during Prime Day, and it has sold for as low as $125.
That’s a great deal on a smart home hub that seamlessly integrates with Alexa and Echo devices, as well as security systems like Ring.
Plus, Apple’s home devices are Matter-compatible, so while there are plenty of gadgets you can pair with them, there are also many you can’t.

If you already own other smart devices or speakers, like an Echo Dot or Echo Show, you won’t be able to link them into a single system, which may mean replacing smaller smart accessories in your home.
Amazon offers several other smart home hubs in various sizes.
I own an iPhone, AirPods, an Apple Watch, and an iPad Air, so I admit, the Apple HomeView looks great on paper.
Apple has finally entered the smart home market with the launch of the HomeView , a direct competitor to the aforementioned brands, and we’ve recently gone hands-on with it.

I got an early look at Apple's new $299 smart home display ahead of its official announcement, and what struck is that HomeView doesn't feel like an iPad attached to a speaker or an oversized Apple Watch.

Instead, it borrows some of the best ideas from across Apple's ecosystem and turns them into something that feels designed specifically for the home, built on a platform Apple is calling “HomeView Software.”
Naturally, HomeView is also designed to manage your smart home.
You can control compatible lights, locks, thermostats and other accessories, create widgets for devices in Apple's Home app, and view up to five security camera feeds simultaneously.
The more I saw of HomeView, the more I realized Apple is serious about giving its smart home ecosystem something it's been missing all along: a centerpiece.
When it comes to controlling smart home devices, an optimally-placed, wall-mounted control center tends to be a preferred interface.
Apple has spent years making products for just about every part of our lives.
There's an iPhone in our pockets, an Apple Watch on our wrists, AirPods in our ears, Macs on our desks and an Apple TV in our living rooms.
But for all its efforts with HomeKit and HomePod, Apple has never really had a defining smart home moment.
The tabletop HomeView comes with a speaker base featuring a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators, along with two full-range drivers in the tilting display itself.
Apple demonstrated its music playback capabilities, including album artwork, lyrics and controls for managing speaker groups.

Sure, Amazon 's Echo Show and Google 's Nest Hub have been around for years, but HomeView is the most inventive new product for Apple users since the Vision Pro — only with a much more approachable price and a purpose that's considerably easier to imagine in everyday life.
No, it's not an entirely new concept for smart displays, but the integration with Apple's existing FaceTime experience could make it especially useful for households that already rely on iPhones.
Between FaceTime, recipes, music, photos and personalized information, there's plenty here for someone who hasn't invested much in smart home technology.
And for those who have, HomeView could be the missing link that brings everything together.
Apple has clearly borrowed some inspiration from the Apple Watch for HomeView's interface, particularly its customizable faces.
Using facial and voice recognition, HomeView can identify up to six people in your household and adjust the information on its screen based on who’s interacting with the display accordingly.
That means schedules, reminders and widgets on the home screen you're looking at can be different from what your partner sees when they approach the same device.
HomeView’s TrueTone display can adjust to the surrounding light, with brightness ranging from 500 nits all the way down to just 0.3 nits.
That's the dimmest display it has ever engineered.
That makes me think a HomeView makes as much sense for your nightstand as it does in those shared high-traffic areas of the house.

Apple’s version of using a smart display into a sous chef relies on a new Safari sub-interface that translates internet recipes into organized, step-by-step instructions.
Apple is also drawing a distinction between accessible shared experiences, like controlling lights or playing music, and private information, like iMessages, Safari browsing and calendar events.
Imagine asking Siri to find a recipe that someone sent you in a text message.
Instead of searching through your conversations, you can ask HomeView to find it using information from your iPhone.
HomeView has a 12MP Center Stage camera and a four-microphone array for hands-free FaceTime calls.
But after witnessing HomeView in action, I'm considerably more interested in having one in my kitchen or on my nightstand than I expected to be.
Apple's smart cameras, thermostats and door locks are expected to launch later this year and in early 2027.

sources.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content
passages: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

passages: As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.
Creators decide what you get, including free trials as well as exclusive episodes, early access, or reduced ads.
You'll even get a badge if you comment on a given episode.
The catch, as you might expect, is Spotify's cut.
The streaming audio service takes 10% of Memberships revenue, so podcasters have to either accept slightly less money or charge more than they do elsewhere.
This is lower than Apple (30% for the first year, 15% after) and YouTube (30%), but it still means some of your spending isn't going to the podcast itself.
It's now easier to support your favorite podcasts beyond listening to ads.
Spotify is launching Memberships, or paid podcast subscriptions, that can provide perks to loyal listeners.
If that concerns you, some podcasts already make subscriptions available beyond Spotify.
Some offer paid access directly through their websites, while others use services like Patreon (which takes a 5% to 12% cut), Ko-Fi (0% to 5%), or Buy Me a Coffee (5%).
The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

The initial batch of Spotify Memberships podcasts include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society , Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows from YMH Studios.
This also helps podcasts extend their reach — they'll theoretically get more paid subscribers than they would if they stuck to the usual crowdfunding methods.
The option is available whether you're a free or Premium user, and you only share contact details with your express permission.
Hosts can access member data that's useful outside of Spotify, so they can tweak their shows based on listening habits.
As such, the in-Spotify approach might be useful simply by keeping shows running or giving them more opportunities to expand.

extraction.body: Spotify is giving podcasters another way to turn loyal listeners into paying supporters, and this time, the offer goes beyond exclusive episodes. The streaming platform has launched a new Memberships feature that allows eligible podcast creators to charge fans for additional benefits directly through Spotify . Instead of relying only on advertising, sponsorships or occasional bonus episodes, creators can build recurring income by offering experiences that make their most dedicated listeners feel closer to their favourite shows. The feature is rolling out across 34 markets, allowing creators to set membership prices and decide what paying fans receive. Spotify says eligible creators will keep 90% of membership revenue, giving podcasters another option for building a sustainable business. Paid podcast subscriptions are not new. Platforms such as Patreon already allow creators to charge fans for exclusive content, behind-the-scenes access and other benefits. Spotify wants to make that experience more accessible by bringing paid memberships directly to its platform, where listeners already discover and stream podcasts. Creators can offer bonus episodes, early access to new releases and reduced advertising. They can also introduce community-focused perks, including member badges and welcome clips, to give subscribers a stronger sense of belonging. That means a podcaster does not necessarily have to produce an entirely separate show to convince listeners to pay. Early access, an ad-light listening experience or a closer connection with the host could be enough to attract some fans. The challenge will be deciding which benefits justify a recurring payment without making free listeners feel as though they are missing out on the entire show. The new membership option is part of Spotify’s wider push to help podcast creators earn money through different channels. Advertising remains an important source of income, but earnings can fluctuate depending on audience size, advertiser demand and the type of content a creator produces. Memberships offer another potential revenue stream because subscribers pay regularly for benefits they value. Spotify is also providing creators with audience insights and promotional tools to help them understand their supporters and grow their memberships. Creators can reach members directly and access tools designed to help them promote their paid offerings. The company also plans to support features such as free trials, giving listeners an opportunity to explore a membership before committing to a payment. This approach puts Spotify in closer competition with Patreon and other membership platforms. However, Spotify’s advantage is that creators can offer paid benefits within an app their audiences may already use every day. The company is not asking podcasters to abandon advertising or sponsorships, either. Memberships can work alongside other revenue streams, giving creators more flexibility in how they fund their shows. The feature could be particularly useful for creators with loyal audiences who regularly return for new episodes. A smaller podcast with an engaged community may find that a group of paying supporters provides more dependable income than chasing larger download numbers alone. Still, not every show will benefit equally. Creators must offer something listeners genuinely value, communicate the benefits clearly and maintain a reliable publishing schedule. A membership becomes harder to justify when subscribers cannot see a clear difference between the free and paid experiences. Eligibility also matters. To qualify for the new feature, podcasters must host their shows through Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 hours of consumption, reach at least 100 listeners or viewers, and have published at least three episodes. The feature is not automatically available to every podcaster. For Nigerian creators, availability is another consideration. Spotify’s podcast monetisation programmes have country-specific eligibility rules, so creators should check the latest requirements before assuming they can activate the new membership feature. Spotify’s move reflects a bigger shift in podcasting. Creators are increasingly looking beyond advertising to build direct relationships with the people who support their work. If listeners are willing to pay for more access, community and convenience, Spotify hopes memberships will help turn that loyalty into recurring revenue. coreStoryFacts.text: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.
As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.
Creators decide what you get, including free trials as well as exclusive episodes, early access, or reduced ads.
You'll even get a badge if you comment on a given episode.
The catch, as you might expect, is Spotify's cut.
The streaming audio service takes 10% of Memberships revenue, so podcasters have to either accept slightly less money or charge more than they do elsewhere.
This is lower than Apple (30% for the first year, 15% after) and YouTube (30%), but it still means some of your spending isn't going to the podcast itself.
It's now easier to support your favorite podcasts beyond listening to ads.
Spotify is launching Memberships, or paid podcast subscriptions, that can provide perks to loyal listeners.
If that concerns you, some podcasts already make subscriptions available beyond Spotify.
Some offer paid access directly through their websites, while others use services like Patreon (which takes a 5% to 12% cut), Ko-Fi (0% to 5%), or Buy Me a Coffee (5%).

The initial batch of Spotify Memberships podcasts include The Adam Friedland Show , Making Sense with Sam Harris , The Shawn Ryan Show , The Sculpt Society , Two Hot Takes , and 12 shows from YMH Studios.
This also helps podcasts extend their reach — they'll theoretically get more paid subscribers than they would if they stuck to the usual crowdfunding methods.
The option is available whether you're a free or Premium user, and you only share contact details with your express permission.
Hosts can access member data that's useful outside of Spotify, so they can tweak their shows based on listening habits.

extraction.body: Spotify is giving podcasters another way to turn loyal listeners into paying supporters, and this time, the offer goes beyond exclusive episodes. The streaming platform has launched a new Memberships feature that allows eligible podcast creators to charge fans for additional benefits directly through Spotify . Instead of relying only on advertising, sponsorships or occasional bonus episodes, creators can build recurring income by offering experiences that make their most dedicated listeners feel closer to their favourite shows. The feature is rolling out across 34 markets, allowing creators to set membership prices and decide what paying fans receive. Spotify says eligible creators will keep 90% of membership revenue, giving podcasters another option for building a sustainable business. Paid podcast subscriptions are not new. Platforms such as Patreon already allow creators to charge fans for exclusive content, behind-the-scenes access and other benefits. Spotify wants to make that experience more accessible by bringing paid memberships directly to its platform, where listeners already discover and stream podcasts. Creators can offer bonus episodes, early access to new releases and reduced advertising. They can also introduce community-focused perks, including member badges and welcome clips, to give subscribers a stronger sense of belonging. That means a podcaster does not necessarily have to produce an entirely separate show to convince listeners to pay. Early access, an ad-light listening experience or a closer connection with the host could be enough to attract some fans. The challenge will be deciding which benefits justify a recurring payment without making free listeners feel as though they are missing out on the entire show. The new membership option is part of Spotify’s wider push to help podcast creators earn money through different channels. Advertising remains an important source of income, but earnings can fluctuate depending on audience size, advertiser demand and the type of content a creator produces. Memberships offer another potential revenue stream because subscribers pay regularly for benefits they value. Spotify is also providing creators with audience insights and promotional tools to help them understand their supporters and grow their memberships. Creators can reach members directly and access tools designed to help them promote their paid offerings. The company also plans to support features such as free trials, giving listeners an opportunity to explore a membership before committing to a payment. This approach puts Spotify in closer competition with Patreon and other membership platforms. However, Spotify’s advantage is that creators can offer paid benefits within an app their audiences may already use every day. The company is not asking podcasters to abandon advertising or sponsorships, either. Memberships can work alongside other revenue streams, giving creators more flexibility in how they fund their shows. The feature could be particularly useful for creators with loyal audiences who regularly return for new episodes. A smaller podcast with an engaged community may find that a group of paying supporters provides more dependable income than chasing larger download numbers alone. Still, not every show will benefit equally. Creators must offer something listeners genuinely value, communicate the benefits clearly and maintain a reliable publishing schedule. A membership becomes harder to justify when subscribers cannot see a clear difference between the free and paid experiences. Eligibility also matters. To qualify for the new feature, podcasters must host their shows through Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 hours of consumption, reach at least 100 listeners or viewers, and have published at least three episodes. The feature is not automatically available to every podcaster. For Nigerian creators, availability is another consideration. Spotify’s podcast monetisation programmes have country-specific eligibility rules, so creators should check the latest requirements before assuming they can activate the new membership feature. Spotify’s move reflects a bigger shift in podcasting. Creators are increasingly looking beyond advertising to build direct relationships with the people who support their work. If listeners are willing to pay for more access, community and convenience, Spotify hopes memberships will help turn that loyalty into recurring revenue. story.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content

facts.text: Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes.
Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube.
Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment.
To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics.
Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.
As with Apple Podcasts and joining a YouTube channel , the Memberships feature lets you pay directly through the show page in the Spotify app.

passages: Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking.
The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number.
The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.
Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers .

With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.
Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer.
Other companies like Meta have also been courting small businesses with AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries .

Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.
The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services.
Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats.

sources.title: Yelp’s AI Assistant Can Call a Restaurant and Join the Waitlist for You - CNET
passages: Just months after launching an updated AI assistant, Yelp Assistant , that can book reservations for you, Yelp is expanding its AI integrations with a new AI agent.
Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes.

As personal and shopping assistants become more widely used, new reports show the hardships faced by both businesses and customers: Businesses must contend with an influx of calls and emails from bots, while human customers must compete with AI agents to make reservations.

“This release is another step forward as we transform Yelp with AI, with updates across every category on Yelp, from booking a table at a restaurant to hiring a pro for a home project,” Akhil Kuduvalli Ramesh, Yelp’s chief product officer, said in a statement.
You can also use Yelp Waitlist to get in line before you arrive.
After you join the line, Yelp Assistant will send you status updates, such as when your table becomes available.
Yelp Assistant’s personalization will also apply to conversations by referencing past chats and your Yelp review history.
For instance, if you’ve recently chatted on Yelp for vegan restaurants near you, the Assistant will ask if you’re interested in more vegan options.
Yelp Assistant now works with OpenTable, allowing you access to thousands of restaurants across the US.
© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.
For further personalization, the app can now reference local weather forecasts when you make reservations, so you don’t book an outdoor patio on a night it’s supposed to pour.
And a new feature, My Lists, lets you save, rank and promote your favorite local businesses, and then Yelp will give you more tailored recommendations based on your lists.
