facts.text: "We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security.
"But companies don't just need to protect the software they build.
AI is making social engineering more convincing and easier to scale, while fundamentally changing how employees work.
With Noon, we're bringing the same approach to workforce security: one platform, less complexity, and protection for every employee, not just those building software."
20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aikido Security today announced the launch of Noon , a dedicated workforce security business that extends its protection beyond software to the people using it.
Noon addresses these threats by bringing email protection, device protection, AI governance and phishing simulation training together in one platform.

Noon's platform is being built on two acquisitions Aikido completed in September 2026: Poland-based Cyberly, founded in 2024, which brought AI-driven attack simulations and AI usage visibility, and Belgium-based Outkept, founded in 2020, which brought email security and phishing awareness training.
Before the acquisitions, Cyberly protected more than 300,000 employees across 200-plus organizations, while Outkept served more than 1,000 organizations and 250,000 users across 100-plus countries.
Aikido's unified security platform secures application testing, code, cloud and runtime, helping teams to reduce risk without slowing down development.

Aikido is the fastest-ever European cybersecurity company to reach unicorn status and is trusted by over 150,000 teams, with a global customer base including SoundCloud, Niantic, Runway, Handshake and Deel.
Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that mobile social engineering attacks, including fraudulent texts and voice calls, succeeded 40% more often than email phishing.
Noon brings employee security into one platform, replacing the separate tools many organizations piece together today:
Yet the security industry has long treated software and workforce security as two separate worlds," said Alex Horlach, co-founder of Cyberly.
The founding teams of both companies continue at Noon.
Cyberly's four co-founders, Alex Horlach, Evgeny Chamtonau, Pavel Hraznykh and Andrew Labadzinski, will continue building the platform.
Most workforce security stacks were built for a different problem: generic phishing emails and scheduled tests.
They also run separately from the tools protecting employee devices or tracking AI usage, leaving security teams managing several disconnected products.
Noon connects directly to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and its results are built to feed into GRC platforms.
Campaign and training data is designed to support audits under frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIS2, DORA, HIPAA and GDPR, and to help meet cyber insurance requirements.

passages: JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE:JPM ) has officially moved its dollar-backed token, JPM Coin (JPMD), to the Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) blockchain.
On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank's blockchain division, made JPM Coin available to select institutional clients on Ethereum's mainnet, which is its primary public blockchain.
This move brings JPM Coin to Ethereum, supplementing its previous version that was launched on Base, a more cost-effective layer-2 network developed by Coinbase Global ( NASDAQ:COIN ).
In Q2 2026, JPMorgan's payments revenue rose 12%, and net interest income rose 10%, though it has not reported specific revenue from JPM Coin.

Existing non-bank stablecoins dominate the dollar token market on Ethereum, and JPMorgan and other major banks reportedly plan a shared tokenized deposit network that could challenge both stablecoins and crypto firms.
So, does JPMorgan's involvement with Ethereum provide ETH holders with a reason to be optimistic about future price increases?
JPMorgan positions JPM Coin as a way for institutions to make payments around the clock, freeing up cash that would typically be tied up outside banking hours.
JPM Coin is essentially a deposit token, where each coin represents a U.S. dollar deposited in a client's account at JPMorgan.

The bank chose the Ethereum network for its greater liquidity than other options and its existing institutional user base. Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs, highlighted this point, although her perspective comes from her role in promoting the product. JPMorgan aims to attract crypto companies looking for blockchain-based payments, as well as financial firms involved in trade settlements or tokenized assets. While Kinexys represents a small portion of JPMorgan's operations, the bank is massive, with $5 trillion in assets and revenue from consumer banking, commercial and investment banking, and asset and wealth management. In Q2 2026, JPMorgan's payments revenue rose 12%, and net interest income rose 10%, though it has not reported specific revenue from JPM Coin. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction ) has officially moved its dollar-backed token, JPM Coin (JPMD), to the Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) blockchain. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain division, made JPM Coin available to select institutional clients on Ethereum’s mainnet , which is its primary public blockchain. This move brings JPM Coin to Ethereum, supplementing its previous version that was launched on Base, a more cost-effective layer-2 network developed by Coinbase Global ( NASDAQ:COIN ). According to Kinexys, it has processed over $4 trillion in transactions since its inception, averaging about $7 billion each day. However, much of this transaction volume occurs on JPMorgan’s private Kinexys network, which operates separately from its public blockchain activities. The bank hasn’t disclosed how much of its total activity occurs on Ethereum or Base. JPM Coin is essentially a deposit token, where each coin represents a U.S. dollar deposited in a client’s account at JPMorgan. This differs from a stablecoin, which is typically backed by a reserve pool managed by a non-bank entity. Despite the launch, ETH did not see a price increase. ETH trades at $2,386, down 4.2% over the past week, 12.3% over the last two weeks, and 51.8% from its all-time high . So, does JPMorgan’s involvement with Ethereum provide ETH holders with a reason to be optimistic about future price increases? Mark Wilson / Getty Images News via Getty Images Importantly, only approved institutional clients can access JPM Coin. Retail investors are unable to buy or hold it, and all holders must have the bank’s approval. JPMorgan positions JPM Coin as a way for institutions to make payments around the clock, freeing up cash that would typically be tied up outside banking hours. The bank chose the Ethereum network for its greater liquidity than other options and its existing institutional user base. Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs, highlighted this point, although her perspective comes from her role in promoting the product. JPMorgan aims to attract crypto companies looking for blockchain-based payments, as well as financial firms involved in trade settlements or tokenized assets. While Kinexys represents a small portion of JPMorgan’s operations, the bank is massive, with $5 trillion in assets and revenue from consumer banking, commercial and investment banking, and asset and wealth management. In Q2 2026, JPMorgan’s payments revenue rose 12%, and net interest income rose 10%, though it has not reported specific revenue from JPM Coin. The deposit-token structure also benefits JPMorgan; when clients hold JPM Coin, the dollars remain on the bank’s balance sheet as deposits. This allows the bank to continue lending those funds and earning interest, even as the cash moves to public blockchains. JPM Coin creates a direct link to ETH because every transaction on the Ethereum mainnet incurs a gas fee, which users pay in ETH. Increased institutional activity on Ethereum could modestly increase demand for ETH to cover these fees. However, each JPM Coin corresponds to one dollar. Clients only need a minimal amount of ETH for transaction fees, and JPMorgan does not require clients to hold ETH as an investment. The bank has not set a volume target for its Ethereum transactions, nor has it disclosed how many clients are utilizing the token on the mainnet. Base serves as a useful reference point. JPM Coin has been active there since November 2025, and Base fees are also paid in ETH. However, JPMorgan has not provided any usage statistics for Base, leaving it unclear how much demand there is for ETH in that context. The competitive landscape further constrains JPM Coin’s potential. Existing non-bank stablecoins dominate the dollar token market on Ethereum, and JPMorgan and other major banks reportedly plan a shared tokenized deposit network that could challenge both stablecoins and crypto firms. Such a network could draw bank activity toward systems they directly control. Market trends also do not indicate a positive outlook. ETH fell by 10.4% in October leading up to October 19. On October 18, it closed 5.9% below its 20-day average and 5.6% below its 50-day average, suggesting a downward trend. Additionally, spot Ether ETFs experienced net outflows of $103 million on October 19, the day JPM Coin launched on Ethereum. This outflow indicates that investors pulled out more money than they added. Notably, BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ:ETHA ) accounted for $95 million of that total. In our view, JPM Coin is unlikely to significantly increase ETH’s price in the near future. JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction ) has officially moved its dollar-backed token, JPM Coin (JPMD), to the Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) blockchain. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain division, made JPM Coin available to select institutional clients on Ethereum’s mainnet , which is its primary public blockchain. This move brings JPM Coin to Ethereum, supplementing its previous version that was launched on Base, a more cost-effective layer-2 network developed by Coinbase Global ( NASDAQ:COIN ).

According to Kinexys, it has processed over $4 trillion in transactions since its inception, averaging about $7 billion each day. However, much of this transaction volume occurs on JPMorgan’s private Kinexys network, which operates separately from its public blockchain activities. The bank hasn’t disclosed how much of its total activity occurs on Ethereum or Base.

JPM Coin is essentially a deposit token, where each coin represents a U.S. dollar deposited in a client’s account at JPMorgan. This differs from a stablecoin, which is typically backed by a reserve pool managed by a non-bank entity.

Despite the launch, ETH did not see a price increase. ETH trades at $2,386, down 4.2% over the past week, 12.3% over the last two weeks, and 51.8% from its all-time high . So, does JPMorgan’s involvement with Ethereum provide ETH holders with a reason to be optimistic about future price increases?
Mark Wilson / Getty Images News via Getty Images

Importantly, only approved institutional clients can access JPM Coin. Retail investors are unable to buy or hold it, and all holders must have the bank’s approval. JPMorgan positions JPM Coin as a way for institutions to make payments around the clock, freeing up cash that would typically be tied up outside banking hours.

The bank chose the Ethereum network for its greater liquidity than other options and its existing institutional user base. Emma Landriault, the head of Kinexys Labs, highlighted this point, although her perspective comes from her role in promoting the product. JPMorgan aims to attract crypto companies looking for blockchain-based payments, as well as financial firms involved in trade settlements or tokenized assets.

While Kinexys represents a small portion of JPMorgan’s operations, the bank is massive, with $5 trillion in assets and revenue from consumer banking, commercial and investment banking, and asset and wealth management. In Q2 2026, JPMorgan’s payments revenue rose 12%, and net interest income rose 10%, though it has not reported specific revenue from JPM Coin.

The deposit-token structure also benefits JPMorgan; when clients hold JPM Coin, the dollars remain on the bank’s balance sheet as deposits. This allows the bank to continue lending those funds and earning interest, even as the cash moves to public blockchains.

JPM Coin creates a direct link to ETH because every transaction on the Ethereum mainnet incurs a gas fee, which users pay in ETH. Increased institutional activity on Ethereum could modestly increase demand for ETH to cover these fees.

However, each JPM Coin corresponds to one dollar. Clients only need a minimal amount of ETH for transaction fees, and JPMorgan does not require clients to hold ETH as an investment. The bank has not set a volume target for its Ethereum transactions, nor has it disclosed how many clients are utilizing the token on the mainnet.

Base serves as a useful reference point. JPM Coin has been active there since November 2025, and Base fees are also paid in ETH. However, JPMorgan has not provided any usage statistics for Base, leaving it unclear how much demand there is for ETH in that context.

The competitive landscape further constrains JPM Coin’s potential. Existing non-bank stablecoins dominate the dollar token market on Ethereum, and JPMorgan and other major banks reportedly plan a shared tokenized deposit network that could challenge both stablecoins and crypto firms. Such a network could draw bank activity toward systems they directly control.

Market trends also do not indicate a positive outlook. ETH fell by 10.4% in October leading up to October 19. On October 18, it closed 5.9% below its 20-day average and 5.6% below its 50-day average, suggesting a downward trend.

Additionally, spot Ether ETFs experienced net outflows of $103 million on October 19, the day JPM Coin launched on Ethereum. This outflow indicates that investors pulled out more money than they added. Notably, BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ:ETHA ) accounted for $95 million of that total.

In our view, JPM Coin is unlikely to significantly increase ETH’s price in the near future. While JPMorgan benefits from 24/7 transaction capabilities, access to crypto-native firms, and deposits that remain on its balance sheet, ETH gains only a large bank’s endorsement and a minor stream of gas fees. Although Ethereum burns a portion of every fee , heavy use is required to meaningfully reduce ETH’s supply.

JPMorgan Asset Management maintained a cautious view of bitcoin in Tuesday’s report, saying its “volatility and unstable correlation to other asset classes…remain an obstacle to [its] widespread inclusion in portfolios.” Furthermore, JPMorgan does not make a case for bitcoin as a portfolio diversifier, instead viewing it as a “speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing,” according to comments by portfolio manager Dr Sheena Shah and head of digital asset strategy Dennis Cristallo. “It lacks a strategic role in portfolios other than as a bet on fiat currency expansion or future asset trading on blockchains,” they added. “BTC mostly trades like a high beta risk asset that tracks global money supply growth, but it is sometimes treated as ‘digital gold.’ Unstable correlations with other assets present a modeling hurdle. extraction.body: Lay’s is bringing the flavors of the holiday dinner table to the snack aisle with five new limited-edition potato chip varieties, including roasted turkey, maple bacon and chocolate-covered chips. The snack brand announced its new “Holi-LAY’S” collection on Monday, Oct. 19, with flavors inspired by traditional holiday dishes and sweet treats. The chips will roll out at stores nationwide and select retailers between late October and December. The five new flavors include three savory options inspired by holiday meals and two sweet varieties featuring chocolate. The new flavors will arrive in phases throughout the holiday season. Lay’s Cheddar Scalloped-Style Potatoes and Roasted Holiday Turkey chips are scheduled to hit shelves nationwide beginning Oct. 25. The Maple Bacon flavor will make its U.S. debut beginning Nov. 8. For those looking for a sweeter snack, Lay’s Wavy Milk Chocolate and Wavy Dubai-Style Dark Chocolate covered potato chips are scheduled to begin appearing at select retailers Dec. 1, with availability expanding in 2027. All five flavors are limited-time offerings. The company is also launching the Happy Holi-LAY’S Sweepstakes on Oct. 26. Fans can scan the code on qualifying Lay’s bags or visit HappyHoli-Lays.com to enter for a chance to win holiday-themed prizes, including branded chip bowls, a charcuterie set, a holiday sweater, a multicooker and a Lay’s collaboration with Le Creuset featuring a signature oval casserole dish. For more information about the new flavors and sweepstakes, visit the official Lay’s website . extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. Rise of cryptocurrency crimes, and how kiosks can play a role Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. States are upping regulations, oversight over crypto ATMs. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Jackson Some of the bill's language includes: Requiring licenses for all kiosk operators under the Money Transmissions Act. It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. You don't have to do that through a gas station. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. We have advocated for a waiting period for first-time customers because it gives time to stop a scam before any funds leave. CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.

Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money.
That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings.
“I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally."

This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine.

The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse.
Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses.
"Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network.
Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether.
This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R).

"HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson

It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000.

North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place.

"We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL.

"Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules."

State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger.

"I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is."

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse. Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. "We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

Generative AI has fundamentally changed hiring. Candidates can tailor resumes, generate cover letters, and apply to hundreds of jobs in minutes. As AI-generated applications become the norm, candidates are submitting nearly 250% more job applications than before ChatGPT, leaving hiring teams to sift through a growing volume of applications while traditional hiring signals like resumes and cover letters become far less meaningful. Juicebox helps companies bypass that process altogether. Rather than waiting for applications to arrive, its AI agents proactively identify, qualify, and engage the right candidates before they ever apply. Juicebox searches more than 800 million profiles across 30+ sources, pulling from unstructured signals such as GitHub, Google Scholar, X, community forums and startup databases to build a more complete picture of each candidate and how well they fit a role. Built from the ground up with AI, Juicebox understands the types of candidates recruiters are looking for in the same way a person does. It can interpret nuanced context around roles and regions, verify that candidate information is still accurate, and learn from a team's prior outreach and hiring decisions so results consistently reflect the company's talent bar. Its AI agents can then handle outreach and follow-ups automatically, while giving teams real-time insights into the talent market. "The talent war costs companies millions," said David Paffenholz, Co-founder and CEO of Juicebox. "Our customers report up to 90% reductions in time spent identifying qualified candidates, helping teams fill roles faster and with higher-quality hires. They've also seen higher recruiter efficiency and more candidate conversations. We're grateful to HR Breakthrough for this award, and we'll continue to enhance our platform to empower recruiters with AI that finds the best-fit candidates faster and more efficiently." The HR Tech Breakthrough Awards program is produced by Tech Breakthrough, the organization behind more than a decade of recognition programs spanning AI, cybersecurity, fintech, digital health, cleantech, edtech, and other technology sectors. The inaugural HR Tech Breakthrough program evaluates solutions across the full spectrum of human resources and workforce technology, from talent acquisition and onboarding to performance management, employee experience, workforce analytics, and beyond. But the companies responding most effectively are the ones proactively identifying and engaging the right candidates before they ever apply," said Steve Johansson, Managing Director at HR Tech Breakthrough. Juicebox is built to scale hiring across an organization, not just speed up one recruiter. We're thrilled to award Juicebox with the award for 'Talent Acquisition Company of the Year.'" Juicebox customers have run more than 600,000 searches and engaged over three million candidates, with adoption from companies including Ramp, Cursor, Lovable, Notion and Samsara. Credit: Penn State . Creative Commons DuBOIS, Pa. — Students, faculty and alumni from Penn State DuBois' Wildlife Technology program participated in two educational hikes on Oct. 4 as part of the annual Walk in Penn's Woods initiative, sharing their knowledge of tree identification, forest management and conservation with local community members and international visitors. During the morning hike at Bilger's Rocks, first-year Wildlife Technology students collaborated with staff from the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources Bureau of Forestry to provide an educational experience focused on tree identification. The hike took place at Bilger's Rocks, which recently became part of Moshannon State Forest, and gave participants an opportunity to learn about the region's trees and other plant species. As part of their coursework, Wildlife Technology students learn to identify more than 100 species of trees, shrubs and vines, developing skills essential to careers in wildlife and natural resource management. Participating in the public hike allowed the students to apply that knowledge outside the classroom while sharing what they have learned with community members. “Experiences like Walk in Penn's Woods give our students an opportunity to take what they're learning in the classroom and apply it in a real-world setting.” Mike Eckley , assistant teaching professor in forestry, Penn State DuBois "Experiences like Walk in Penn's Woods give our students an opportunity to take what they're learning in the classroom and apply it in a real-world setting," Mike Eckley, assistant teaching professor in forestry at Penn State DuBois said. "They're not only strengthening their knowledge of the natural environment, but also developing the communication and professional skills they'll need as the next generation of wildlife and natural resource managers." Later that afternoon, Penn State DuBois Wildlife Technology faculty and alumni led a forest management-focused hike at Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake for a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania through the American Hardwood Export Council (AHEC). The journalists were visiting Pennsylvania as part of the production of "Forested Future," a film highlighting the sustainability, management and stewardship of American hardwood forests. Their visit to Treasure Lake provided an opportunity to showcase regional forest management practices, wildlife habitat improvements and partnerships supporting responsible forestry. Eckley led the hike alongside recent Penn State graduate Elizabeth Bruner, who now works for the Pennsylvania Game Commission. Together, they discussed differences between public and private land management and explained how forestry practices contribute to healthy forest ecosystems. Penn State alumna Elizabeth Bruner shares her knowledge during a hike at the Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake, in Clearfield County. The hike was attended by a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania. Credit: Penn State . Creative Commons The hike highlighted recently completed forestry practices at Community Woodlands, where partnerships with Domtar Paper Company, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Ruffed Grouse Society and Audubon Mid-Atlantic have supported forest management and conservation efforts. Through these partnerships, the project has supported timber stand improvement, wildlife habitat creation and invasive species removal. Eckley has also involved Penn State fisheries, wildlife and forestry students in the work, providing hands-on opportunities to learn about forest management and conservation. The forest management project has also included the salvage harvesting of two American chestnut trees from the property. The Allegheny Hardwood Utilization Group, whose executive director, Amy Shields, helped arrange the journalists' visit, coordinated kiln drying of the lumber through Forcey Lumber in Woodland. Shields also serves on the Wildlife Technology program's advisory board and has supported student professional development through summer internship opportunities. Eckley plans to work with Pennsylvania forest and wood products organizations to create commemorative pieces from the lumber in recognition of America's 250th anniversary. A special preliminary showing of "Forested Future," a video production featuring Pennsylvania forests, local footage and interviews with natural resource professionals, is being planned for later this winter at Penn State DuBois. Students, faculty, staff and community members will be invited to attend, with additional details to be announced as plans are finalized. Together, the two hikes demonstrated how Penn State DuBois' Wildlife Technology program connects classroom learning with practical experience while supporting conservation education and responsible forest management. Through partnerships with government agencies, industry professionals and conservation organizations, the program continues to provide students with opportunities to develop their skills, engage with the community and contribute to the stewardship of Pennsylvania's natural resources.

DuBOIS, Pa. — Students, faculty and alumni from Penn State DuBois' Wildlife Technology program participated in two educational hikes on Oct. 4 as part of the annual Walk in Penn's Woods initiative, sharing their knowledge of tree identification, forest management and conservation with local community members and international visitors.

During the morning hike at Bilger's Rocks, first-year Wildlife Technology students collaborated with staff from the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources Bureau of Forestry to provide an educational experience focused on tree identification. The hike took place at Bilger's Rocks, which recently became part of Moshannon State Forest, and gave participants an opportunity to learn about the region's trees and other plant species.

As part of their coursework, Wildlife Technology students learn to identify more than 100 species of trees, shrubs and vines, developing skills essential to careers in wildlife and natural resource management. Participating in the public hike allowed the students to apply that knowledge outside the classroom while sharing what they have learned with community members.
“Experiences like Walk in Penn's Woods give our students an opportunity to take what they're learning in the classroom and apply it in a real-world setting.”
Mike Eckley , assistant teaching professor in forestry, Penn State DuBois

"Experiences like Walk in Penn's Woods give our students an opportunity to take what they're learning in the classroom and apply it in a real-world setting," Mike Eckley, assistant teaching professor in forestry at Penn State DuBois said. "They're not only strengthening their knowledge of the natural environment, but also developing the communication and professional skills they'll need as the next generation of wildlife and natural resource managers."

Later that afternoon, Penn State DuBois Wildlife Technology faculty and alumni led a forest management-focused hike at Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake for a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania through the American Hardwood Export Council (AHEC).

The journalists were visiting Pennsylvania as part of the production of "Forested Future," a film highlighting the sustainability, management and stewardship of American hardwood forests. Their visit to Treasure Lake provided an opportunity to showcase regional forest management practices, wildlife habitat improvements and partnerships supporting responsible forestry.

Eckley led the hike alongside recent Penn State graduate Elizabeth Bruner, who now works for the Pennsylvania Game Commission. Together, they discussed differences between public and private land management and explained how forestry practices contribute to healthy forest ecosystems.

Penn State alumna Elizabeth Bruner shares her knowledge during a hike at the Community Woodlands at Treasure Lake, in Clearfield County. The hike was attended by a group of international journalists visiting Pennsylvania. Credit: Penn State . Creative Commons

The hike highlighted recently completed forestry practices at Community Woodlands, where partnerships with Domtar Paper Company, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Ruffed Grouse Society and Audubon Mid-Atlantic have supported forest management and conservation efforts.

Through these partnerships, the project has supported timber stand improvement, wildlife habitat creation and invasive species removal. Eckley has also involved Penn State fisheries, wildlife and forestry students in the work, providing hands-on opportunities to learn about forest management and conservation.

The forest management project has also included the salvage harvesting of two American chestnut trees from the property. The Allegheny Hardwood Utilization Group, whose executive director, Amy Shields, helped arrange the journalists' visit, coordinated kiln drying of the lumber through Forcey Lumber in Woodland. Shields also serves on the Wildlife Technology program's advisory board and has supported student professional development through summer internship opportunities.
Eckley plans to work with Pennsylvania forest and wood products organizations to create commemorative pieces from the lumber in recognition of America's 250th anniversary.

A special preliminary showing of "Forested Future," a video production featuring Pennsylvania forests, local footage and interviews with natural resource professionals, is being planned for later this winter at Penn State DuBois. Students, faculty, staff and community members will be invited to attend, with additional details to be announced as plans are finalized.

Together, the two hikes demonstrated how Penn State DuBois' Wildlife Technology program connects classroom learning with practical experience while supporting conservation education and responsible forest management. Through partnerships with government agencies, industry professionals and conservation organizations, the program continues to provide students with opportunities to develop their skills, engage with the community and contribute to the stewardship of Pennsylvania's natural resources.

passages: Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak.

Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.
Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies .
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable.
They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways.

In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.
It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task.
That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both.
OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products.
He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.
But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound.
The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies .
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable.
They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways.

In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.
It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task.
That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both.
OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products.
He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.
But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound.
The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents , a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”
When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.
Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.
This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies . The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents , which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.
